## Outer workflow handler cancellation boundary — 2026-10-06

Production outer handlers and named continuations now run behind a cancellable
boundary. On cancellation without joining, the delivery returns without reading
or mutating the SDK/journal buffers still owned by the abandoned handler; its
late result is discarded. Durable cancellation remains retained for the next
redelivery. SDK appends reject their cancelled context before accessing the
append closure. Panic behavior stays bounded; outer runtime.Goexit now records
an Attempt and follows the existing three-attempt terminal policy. Go cannot
stop ignored cancellation externally; downstream idempotency remains required.

Race controls cover normal return/error, panic, Goexit, already-cancelled entry
and late return/panic/Goexit after abandonment. Modeled production-worker handoff
passes1,000 seeds across parent cancellation, closed heartbeat and lost renewal
ack, with10 exact replays: successor42 wins, late SDK append rejected, full journal
unchanged and retained integrity1/4/1 with physical model queue empty. Three
existing worker execution/running-cancel/heartbeat suites pass their1,000 race
schedules and replay checks. Native fresh R3 Goexit control passes7.594s with
Started,three Attempt and Failed records. Its initial20s fixture attempt failed
in provisioning before any handler ran; corrected startup waits for metadata
readiness with bounded requests inside the same20s whole-test context. Preliminary
SIM_SEEDS=100 was rejected by the existing minimum1000 gate; only the corrected
full1,000 runs count. The new handoff regression rejects pre-fix ca7a1fa via a compiler overlay at seed1
with the explicit trapped-delivery3s deadline error; only in-memory transport used.
[Controls](scale/outer-handler-cancellation-2026-10-06/). Full-suite and broader native/combined qualification remain
open; no promotion of current-main full matrices or earlier recorded-source runs.

The current100k gate, sustained ahead20/200 acceptance, full200-seed Tier2 matrix,
full Tier3 matrix/24h soak, the sustained whole-chaos mutation campaign and combined timer-cut/
continuation cases remain open. Running campaigns and component proofs do not
clear these gates. The sections below retain chronological evidence and failures.
The planned increase to10k per commit is not implemented; the plan conditions
that increase on completing within a few minutes on CI hardware. The current
incremental gate is1k, while accepted100k campaigns apply only to their recorded
source graphs.

This records what the current repository proves. The [implementation plan](implementation-plan.md) remains the release target. Its Tier 1 section specifies a seeded, replayable in-memory transport model, differential contract checks against real NATS, and incremental proof gates. The seeded and differential results below cover several transport slices, including short worker execution, signal resume, native timer wakeup, and fallback timer scan-to-worker wakeup; other integrated paths remain unfinished.

One [clean-runner integration job](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36660121227) found a blob-sweep differential mismatch after purging retained references: the real Object Store pass listed and deleted one object while the model listed and deleted five. The first retained-reference pass had matched, and 35 focused local repeats of the contract passed; the cause is unconfirmed. On the next mismatch the contract now records a second Object Store listing, individual `GetInfo` results for all seven fixture names, and the raw object-stream state so a partial listing can be distinguished from missing or deleted metadata. This does not count as a clean differential gate.

The long-journal read optimization now has a Tier 1 transport boundary: the same production read loop uses either a real filtered JetStream pull consumer or an in-memory cursor after 64 serial entries. A new 1,000-seed workload covers no-responder and consumer-deleted replies before or after partial delivery, cursor replacement, bounded exhaustion, interleaved subjects, a deleted middle entry with virtual whole-read retries and `ErrGap`, exact replay, and cross-process trace identity. A local 100,000-seed run of that workload passed in 167.62 seconds; this is one slice, not the full release gate. The [expanded 10,000-seed-per-workload CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36619017173) passed 500,602 total schedules at `46d5056` in 7m3.8s of Go test time. The three-node 300-entry contract mirrors the publish order in the model and compares all reconstructed records and the tail, then deletes a real middle entry to verify `ErrGap`. The focused real-cluster test and complete `journal` and `sim` package suites passed locally. The clean [100,000-entry boundary](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36618655746) read all entries in 604 ms, and the [repeated 5,000-entry snapshot control](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36618655971) passed three runs at `adb4ce9` after the batch-port refactor.

The [expanded 100,000-seed-per-workload CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36619464017) passed at `e82897b`: model version 3 generated 5,000,602 schedules, 150,227,003 scheduler choices, and 1,177,902,920 transport events in 59m20.3s of Go test time. This clears the release seed-count gate for the expanded modeled slices, including long-journal reads; remaining Tier 1 transport edges and the independent real-cluster gates remain open.

A [later 100,000-seed-per-workload clean-runner run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36661347183) passed at `14a0038`: 5,200,603 generated schedules, 150,951,853 scheduler choices, and 1,260,019,228 transport events in 37m22.0s of Go test time. It includes the seeded 10158 signal pipeline but predates the ten-second suspended-wakeup retry and its lost-NAK transport replay. A new release-count run for those additions is in progress below.

The focused five-node container smoke, verified server/worker clock-skew, worker-recovery, and rolling-upgrade workflows are now scheduled daily at 05:17, 05:37, 05:57, and 06:17 UTC respectively. Scheduled container runs use the same `2m` file-store sync interval as the manual default, and all four retain their manual triggers. Their first scheduled executions and the plan's sustained 24-hour full-matrix Tier 3 soak remain open.

A new opt-in five-container Tier 3 test SIGKILLs an actual worker process after its `StepRequested` entry is durable and its effect has started, then runs a replacement worker pinned to a different NATS node. Three local repeats and one race-instrumented run each completed with one invocation, four ordered journal entries, one terminal result, a higher replacement fencing epoch, and passing `Start` and `Await` histories. A further local run added a duplicate `Start` and a second terminal read through the replacement node; both passed the same history models. The [clean five-container CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36621543073) passed all five tests, and its downloaded history artifact contains one successful start, one matching duplicate, and two terminal reads with the same result hash. Kill-to-terminal times were 31.11–31.12 seconds locally and 31.109 seconds in CI. These historical runs used a 30-second lease TTL: their 31.1-second recovery is a fixture configuration mismatch, not evidence of a runtime defect. The current smoke provisions the production 12-second TTL and retains the under-30-second recovery gate. No further runs should chase the old TTL-bound miss. The historical runs remain partial evidence and do not count as a green current-source matrix cell.

A Tier 1 replay of this worker-kill timing runs production lease acquisition and journal append decisions against virtual KV and journal transports. At 29,999 ms the replacement gets `ErrHeld`; at 30,000 ms it acquires a higher epoch and completes the journal. Exact replay, the full simulator package, and the focused race test passed. This establishes the configured TTL as a lower bound in the modeled failure, while the real run's extra ~1.1 seconds remains client scheduling, redelivery, and server work that the model does not isolate.

The same Tier 1 lease-bound replay now advances to 45,000 ms, modeling the paused owner resuming after the successor's terminal write. Production `lease.Renew` returns `ErrLost`, production journal `Append` rejects the old epoch and tail with `ErrStale`, and a read confirms the four-entry journal is byte-for-byte unchanged. The trace is pinned in the regression corpus; exact disk replay, the full simulator package, and the focused race test pass. This checks the production fencing decisions observed in the five-container pause run; the model does not simulate the actual process stop, heartbeat goroutine, or NATS leader behavior.

A second opt-in Tier 3 five-container test commits six child requests and the parent suspension, stops its worker, SIGKILLs all five NATS containers with the configured `sync_interval=2m`, and restarts them on the same file stores. It requires exactly six distinct child IDs, immutable parent and child results through restarted pinned nodes, a duplicate `Start` response, passing `Start` and `Await` histories, and seven terminal invocations in the raw-state audit. Five repeated local runs with the 30-second recovery-p99 assertion passed; their measured p99 values from confirmed route recovery for children and last-child completion for the parent were 3.02–5.06 seconds. A race-instrumented run passed at 5.60 seconds. An earlier diagnostic race run, before per-invocation timestamps were added, observed the parent result 45.43 seconds after metadata and route readiness; it did not capture the last child's terminal timestamp, so its cause and corresponding plan-defined p99 remain unconfirmed. The five-container result is a fan-out/full-restart matrix slice, not the full matrix or 24-hour soak.

The [clean five-container fan-out CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36623859107) passed the full manual smoke suite at `4cddbef`: six children and the parent were terminal after all five server processes restarted, with a measured plan-defined p99 of 3.04 seconds and a seven-invocation raw-state audit.

A third opt-in five-container slice suspends 16 native timers, verifies each `fire_at` and retained schedule, SIGKILLs all five servers before any timer is due, then restarts the same stores with `sync_interval=2m`. A replacement worker completes all 16 no earlier than their deadlines; the test checks `Start` and `Await` histories, an 80-entry terminal-journal audit, and p99 from the later of `fire_at` and confirmed route recovery. The first attempt reached a `WF_RUN` stream lookup that consumed its five-minute context after restart; the server-side cause is unconfirmed because that attempt did not save logs. The fixture now uses bounded five-replica stream and consumer readiness checks before the lookup and captures each server log tail on failure. Four subsequent local runs, including three repeated runs and one race run, passed with p99 235–267 ms, 16 invocations, 16 journals, 80 entries, and 16 terminal results. This is a small timer/full-restart matrix slice, not the 1,000-timer three-node scale proof or the full Tier 3 matrix.

The [clean five-container timer CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36625842980) passed at `e37a6ce` with all 16 terminal invocations, a 271.7 ms plan-defined p99, and a 32-operation Start/Await history artifact. The same suite's fan-out/full-restart slice passed at a 5.25-second p99.

A fourth opt-in five-container slice publishes 16 ordered signals to a suspended invocation, SIGKILLs all five servers, verifies those retained signals after the five replicas recover, then publishes 16 more and resumes on a worker pinned to another node. It checks a matching retry and changed-payload rejection across the restart, all 32 consumed signal sequences and payloads, cross-node immutable result reads, Porcupine `Start`, `Signal`, and `Await` histories, and the raw-state audit. The first local attempt called the five-replica readiness helper before the durable run consumer existed; moving it after the partition loop started fixed the fixture. The original version stopped its first worker before signal publication and passed four normal runs and a race run with a 99-entry terminal journal. Two later local runs passed the under-30-second terminal latency gate from the exact last enabling signal at 206 and 213 ms.

The [first clean five-container signal CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36626771487) passed the full suite at `d00bf1a` and retained all 32 ordered signals through the restart, with a 37-operation Start/Signal/Await history artifact. That revision did not yet enforce the terminal latency gate.

The [exact-timestamp clean five-container CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36627497362) passed the full suite at `53c7609`. Its signal terminal latency was 315 ms from the last enabling signal, and its downloaded 37-operation history artifact passed the Start, Signal, and Await models.

The signal fixture now keeps its first worker running until it has consumed the first 16 signals and suspended again. It saves the exact journal prefix, verifies that prefix is unchanged immediately after the five-server restart, then lets the replacement consume the remaining 16. Three local normal runs and one race-instrumented run passed with a 102-entry terminal journal and 111–225 ms recovery from the last enabling signal. The [clean five-container CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36628996662) passed the full suite at `3712dd7`: the signal slice recovered in 212 ms, retained all 32 ordered consumptions, and produced a 37-operation client-history artifact. This exercises resumed handler replay across the restart; the broader signal fault matrix remains open.

A fifth opt-in five-container slice starts ten short workflows on one durable `WF_RUN` partition, blocks the first journaled effect, then SIGKILLs the actual consumer leader while the worker remains pinned to a surviving node. It confirms a different consumer leader is elected before releasing the effect, requires each effect to execute once, reads all ten immutable results from the surviving worker node and the restarted former leader, checks Start/Await histories, and audits ten invocations, ten journals, 40 entries, and ten terminals. Four normal local runs and one race run passed; the slowest terminal result after confirmed new-leader election was 121–247 ms. This covers one consumer-leader kill during active execution, not the every-30-second mixed workload row or full Tier 3 matrix.

The [clean five-container consumer-leader CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36630685206) passed the full manual suite at `2acf88a`. The new consumer leader was confirmed before the blocked effect resumed; all ten workflows finished once, the slowest result arrived 429 ms after election, the raw-state audit found 40 entries and ten terminals, and the downloaded artifact contained 30 Start/Await operations.

The clock-skew harness now has a fail-closed server injector. A local `libfaketime` probe moved `date` by +60 seconds but left both static and cgo Go `time.Now` unshifted, so that preload would not exercise this pinned Go server. An opt-in Docker fixture instead builds the same NATS source with a test-only Go `time.Now` wall-clock overlay on one node and checks the actual `/varz` clock before a workload. A three-container probe measured the targeted server at +59.999 seconds while its peers remained unshifted. The five-container test then preferred that node as `WF_RUN` leader, checked its measured ±60-second clock, the journaled `fire_at`, the leader before and after, Start/Await histories, the five-entry terminal journal, and the raw-state audit. Two repeated local runs and a race run passed both skew directions: three-second native sleeps completed in 3.107–3.119 seconds of real time. A further run added a two-second server-clock lateness gate and passed at 98–99 ms. The default unskewed five-container consumer-leader test also passed after the fixture change. The [clean five-container CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36635729258) passed both offsets at `55218ea`: measured server offsets were +59.999 and −60.001 seconds, real timer durations were 3.108 and 3.105 seconds, and server-clock lateness was 98.8 and 98.4 ms. Its artifact contains two Start/Await history operations per direction. The test changes Go's wall clock in the test server binary; larger mixed workloads remain open.

The same fail-closed Go overlay now builds a separate child worker process at ±5 seconds while all five NATS containers retain their real clocks. The child measures its own `time.Now` against an unshifted server's `/varz` before accepting work. Both local directions passed: measured offsets were +5.001 and −4.999 seconds, and three-second native sleeps completed in 3.108 seconds each. Each direction passed a server-clock deadline and under-two-second lateness check (103 and 98 ms), Start/Await Porcupine checks, a five-entry terminal journal, and a one-invocation raw-state audit. The [combined clean five-container CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36636600432) passed server offsets of +59.999 and −60.001 seconds and worker offsets of +5.002 and −4.999 seconds at `f27bd42`. All four three-second timers finished in 3.106–3.109 seconds with 97–98 ms server-clock lateness. Its downloaded artifact contains two Start/Await operations for each direction, eight records in total. These are one timer cell each of the worker- and server-skew matrix rows; the other workload cells remain open.

The ±5-second skewed worker now also consumes 16 ordered signals on a second invocation in the same five-container run. It checks matching-key retry and changed-payload rejection, every retained `SignalConsumed` sequence and payload, Start/Signal/Await Porcupine histories, and both terminal journals through a raw-state audit. Both normal and race-instrumented local runs passed both directions: each timer remained within 95–104 ms of its server deadline, each signal invocation completed 113–116 ms after the final enabling signal, and each run retained two invocations, two journals, and two immutable results. The signal journal had 52 or 53 entries depending on suspension timing, all 16 consumptions were ordered. The [clean five-container CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36638175094) passed both worker offsets at `4b7134c`: timer lateness was 96–100 ms, both 16-signal invocations completed 108–109 ms after the final enabling signal, and the raw-state audit found two invocations, two journals, 57 entries, and two terminals per direction. Its downloaded artifact contains 22 Start/Signal/Await operations for each worker direction; the unchanged ±60-second server-timer slices passed too.

The ±60-second server-skew slice now also places the `WF_SIG` stream leader on the skewed node alongside `WF_RUN` and drives 16 ordered signals through a second invocation. It verifies both leaders before the workload and the signal leader afterward, matching-key retry and changed-payload rejection, every journaled consumption, Start/Signal/Await histories, and a two-invocation raw-state audit. One normal and one race-instrumented local run passed both directions: server-clock timer lateness was 97–101 ms, signal completion was 109–220 ms after the last enabling signal, and each run retained two invocations, two journals, 57 entries, and two terminal results. The [clean combined five-container CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36638863645) passed at `fe189b6`: server offsets were +59.999 and −60.001 seconds, worker offsets were +5.001 and −4.998 seconds, all four timer latencies from their server deadlines were 97–99 ms, and each of the four 16-signal invocations completed 112–115 ms after the last enabling send. All four raw-state audits found two invocations, two journals, 57 entries, and two terminals; the artifact contains 22 Start/Signal/Await operations for each direction, 88 total. This proves the timer and signal cells for these focused workloads; short and fan-out cells and the sustained matrix remain open.

Both clock-skew slices now add 100 distinct short workflows whose handlers execute a journaled `wf.Run` effect. The worker-skew slice runs the handlers in the offset child process. The server-skew slice elects the offset node as leader of `WF_JRN` and `KV_WF_STATE` as well as `WF_RUN` and `WF_SIG` before starting the batch, then confirms the journal and state leaders remained there. Every short invocation has one `Started`, `StepRequested`, `StepCompleted`, and `Completed` entry, one expected result from the control node and the same result through another node. Start/Await histories and a raw-state audit cover all 102 invocations per direction, including the timer and signal. Local normal runs passed with start-to-terminal-read p99 of 1.83–2.02 seconds; one race-instrumented run passed all four directions with p99 of 2.09–2.90 seconds. Each retained audit found 102 invocations, 102 journals, 457 entries, and 102 terminals. The [clean five-container CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36639955906) passed all four directions at `4390330`: short-workflow p99 was 1.04–1.07 seconds, signal completion was 105–107 ms after the last enabling send, and server-clock timer lateness was 98–101 ms. Its downloaded artifact contains 222 Start/Signal/Await operations for each direction, 888 total. This adds a focused short-workflow cell for each skew row; fan-out and sustained mixed workloads remain open.

The clock-skew slices now also run a six-child `CallAsync`/`AwaitPromise` fan-out in each direction. After six distinct child IDs and the parent suspension are durable, child workers run only the needed partitions; in the ±5-second case a second Go-overlay child process verifies its own skew before handling those partitions. Every child has one four-entry `wf.Run` effect journal and the expected result, the parent journal has six child requests and six consumed result signals, and the parent and children return the same immutable results through another NATS node. The parent terminal message's `WF_JRN` server timestamp follows the last child terminal timestamp by 14–80 ms across normal and race-instrumented local runs. The ±60-second case verifies `WF_RUN`, `WF_SIG`, `WF_JRN`, and `KV_WF_STATE` leaders remain on the skewed node through fan-out. All four local directions passed Start/Signal/Await histories and a raw-state audit of 109 invocations, 109 journals, 515–517 entries, and 109 terminals. The [clean combined five-container CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36641131607) passed at `6c8dd84`: verified server offsets were +59.998 and −60.001 seconds, worker offsets were +5.001 and −4.999 seconds, six children completed in each direction, and the parent terminal followed the last child by 39–77 ms. Its raw-state audits found 109 invocations, 109 journals, 515–516 entries, and 109 terminals per direction; its downloaded artifact contains 224 Start/Signal/Await operations per direction, 896 total. These are focused four-workload skew slices, while sustained mixed skew and the rest of the fault matrix remain open.

A sixth opt-in five-container slice pauses a separate worker process with `SIGSTOP` after a journaled `StepRequested` enters its effect, keeps it stopped for 45 seconds past the 30-second lease TTL, and runs a successor pinned to another NATS node. The successor writes the only `StepCompleted` and immutable terminal result under a higher fencing epoch. After `SIGCONT`, the old effect returns an error; the four-entry journal and terminal result remain unchanged. Three normal local runs and one race-instrumented run passed with a 45-second pause, 31.106–31.118 seconds from pause to successor terminal, passing Start/Await histories, and a one-invocation raw-state audit. As with the worker-kill slice, the lease TTL makes the fault-to-terminal time exceed the plan's under-30-second p99 target; this is a safety pass and an open latency gate. The full pause/fault matrix remains open.

The [first clean five-container pause CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36632501474) passed the full suite at `2e1dfb9`: the successor completed 31.108 seconds after pause, and the resumed old handler returned `context canceled` without changing retained state. Its three-operation Start/Await history artifact passed. That revision did not require a fencing counter. The paused child now also reports its production worker fencing counter after resuming; one additional local run and a race run passed with `fencing_events=1`, the old handler's `ErrLost`, and the same immutable result. The [metric-gated clean CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36632861321) passed the full suite at `0bb3e70`: the child reported `fencing_events=1` and `ErrLost`, and the successor completed 31.108 seconds after pause.

New-cluster `WF_LEASE` provisioning now uses a 20-second TTL with the existing five-second renewal heartbeat. The five-container SIGKILL and 45-second `SIGSTOP` tests now assert the under-30-second fault-to-successor-terminal gate instead of only logging it. Local normal runs passed at 21.010 and 21.008 seconds; race-instrumented runs passed at 21.029 and 21.117 seconds. The pause run still recorded one production fencing event, `ErrLost` from the resumed old handler, one immutable terminal result, and a four-entry journal. A three-node test changed an otherwise matching `WF_LEASE` bucket back to 30 seconds, verified `provision.Ensure` rejected it, then explicitly restored 20 seconds and verified provisioning succeeded. Existing deployments must stop lease holders and explicitly change that bucket TTL before running this version; the provisioner does not migrate it. The [clean five-container worker recovery workflow](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36642201086) passed at `841290f`: kill-to-terminal was 21.009 seconds, pause-to-successor-terminal was 21.010 seconds, and the resumed old worker reported `ErrLost` and one fencing event with an unchanged four-entry terminal journal. These are focused single-invocation fault cells; the multi-invocation p99 matrix remains open.

The pinned Tier 1 worker-kill/worker-pause trace now takes its virtual KV expiry from `provision.LeaseTTL`. It confirms the successor is held at 19,999 ms, acquires at 20,000 ms, and the old owner cannot renew or append when resumed at 45,000 ms. The generated trace, exact disk replay, and focused race test pass, keeping the deterministic lease boundary aligned with the five-container tests.

The three-node lease TTL migration contract now creates a retained lease entry before changing the bucket from 20 to 30 seconds and back. It verifies the same value and KV revision through other nodes after both updates, while the provisioner rejects the old TTL between them. A focused local run passed; this tests data preservation for the manual bucket update without weakening the stop-lease-holders migration requirement.

The 200-invocation, 50-journaled-step combined fault test also passed locally with the new 20-second lease in 183.75 seconds; a race-instrumented run passed in 213.41 seconds. Six workers experienced an in-flight process `SIGKILL`, a 45-second `SIGSTOP`, a 45-second worker connection cut, and a 45-second server route partition while assignments moved 96 times, including 22 and 32 moves during active handlers in the respective runs. All 200 results equaled 50, the paused worker's stale append was rejected, the run queue drained, and the retained-state checker found 20,400 journal entries in each run. These remain two combined-fault runs, shorter and less frequent than the plan's five-minute fault-every-two-seconds proof.

The combined 200-workflow rebalance test now runs as a separate job on every push and pull request. Its [first clean-runner job](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36655982268) passed at `a596d12`. It exercises the overlapping process kill, process pause, worker connection cut, and route partition together; it does not substitute for the full fault matrix or the five-minute fault-every-two-seconds run.

A [later rebalance CI job](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36656280938) completed the workload but failed its paused-worker fencing probe: the old worker's one-shot append reported an unknown outcome after a ten-second stream lookup timeout instead of a definitive stale-epoch rejection. A [second clean-runner job](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36658357327) failed at the same probe. The child probe now retries transient unknown and deadline outcomes for at most 45 seconds, reusing the old epoch and tail. Any successful stale append still fails the test. The first local combined run with this retry reached all 200 completed workflows and the stale append check, then exhausted its four-minute overall context while asking `WF_RUN` whether the queue had drained; it did not establish the queue state. With a six-minute fixture context and the unchanged seven-minute CI test timeout, the next local run passed in 149.39 seconds: 200 results, 68 assignment moves, 18 during active handlers, a definitive stale append, a drained queue, and 20,400 journal entries. The [first clean-runner job with both changes](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36659105004) passed. This is one green CI run after two probe failures; the larger rebalance matrix remains open.

Three subsequent clean-runner combined-rebalance jobs ([one](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36660121227), [two](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36660257248), [three](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36660833171)) completed the workload but again exhausted the 45-second stale-token probe through its pinned NATS node; the [next job](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36661085821) passed. The resumed child now tries its original connection first, then rotates new connections through the other two nodes on transient unknown or deadline outcomes, preserving the same old epoch and tail for every append. A local combined-fault run passed in 163.92 seconds with 200 completions, 80 assignment moves, 16 during active handlers, a definitive stale append, a drained queue, and 20,400 entries. This tests the stale token through a healthy peer when the pinned node does not answer; clean-runner validation of the revised probe remains open.

The [clean 20-seed mixed Tier 2 run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36642513177) passed all consecutive seeds 1–20 at `c2875da` with the 20-second lease. Every seed completed and audited its ten-parent/six-child, four-server-fault fixture, and every last-enabling-event terminal p99 stayed below 30 seconds; the slowest was 14.532 seconds at seed 11. This checks the shorter lease against the existing mixed slice, not the ten-minute-per-seed full matrix or a new 200-seed release run.

The expanded mixed fixture now uses eight native timers per timer invocation, 16 ordered signals per signal invocation, and a two-level fan-out with six children and 12 grandchildren. Its [first 20-seed clean-runner run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36654679970) completed and audited all 28 invocations in seeds 1–20, but seed 20 failed the under-30-second terminal p99 gate: one signal invocation completed 37.56 seconds after its last committed signal. The same seed passed locally four times at 9.42–17.23 seconds, so the schedule does not reproduce the delay by itself. The clean-runner failure showed heavy lease contention and redeliveries; the exact delay source is unconfirmed. Failure-only diagnostics now report each slow signal invocation's retained journal times and worker IDs. A [second 20-seed clean-runner run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36655113633) passed the expanded workload, with its slowest p99 at 20.78 seconds in seed 20. This establishes one clean expanded run but does not erase the earlier latency failure; later runs are still active.

A [later clean-runner run with those diagnostics](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36655982319) failed at seed 2: one signal invocation took 34.81 seconds from its last committed signal to terminal. Its retained journal shows the original worker consumed eight signals, suspended at +9.23 seconds, and the replacement worker did not commit the next consumption until +30.01 seconds. The 20.78-second gap is close to the configured 20-second consumer `AckWait`; the trace does not establish whether a NAK, release, or wakeup was lost. The fixture previously omitted the production signal reconciler. It now performs a post-heal `SignalScan` repair pass after sending the signal batch. Local replays of seeds 2 and 20 passed at terminal p99 15.87 and 16.24 seconds; the scanner inspected 41 and 42 signals and reenqueued 15 and 26 still unconsumed signals respectively. The [first clean-runner 20-seed run with that single pass](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36656663286) failed at seed 17: a fan-out child took 36.63 seconds after its last grandchild completed, and a signal invocation had a 20.72-second gap between suspension and its next consumption. The signal pass occurred before these later waits became ready. The fixture now also runs the production `SuspendedScan` loop after heal so it can repair waits as they become ready. One local replay with a 128-invocation scan budget passed seed 17 at p99 26.44 seconds, but a race-instrumented replay failed at 32.58 seconds; its child journal recorded the next consumption only 31.30 seconds after the last grandchild completed. The loop's per-scan context is five seconds, so a 128-invocation scan under injected disk delay may expire without advancing its cursor. Reducing this fixture's scan budget to eight gave seed 17 p99 values of 11.73 seconds under the race detector and 29.04 and 18.17 seconds in two normal repeats. This is evidence for a scan-budget sensitivity, not a confirmed root cause or a closed clean-runner gate; the production CLI still defaults to a 500-sequence budget.

The [first 20-seed CI run with the eight-invocation suspended scan](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36658357280) passed seeds 1–18, then failed seed 19 before its terminal audit when `SignalScan` tried to publish a wakeup whose message ID was concurrently in process on the server. The [next clean-runner run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36659105107) hit the same error at seed 4. JetStream error 10158 is [defined as a duplicate message ID in process](https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/blob/main/server/jetstream_errors_generated.go). `Client.Enqueue` and the signal wakeup path now retry that exact message ID for at most two seconds and 80 conflicts; every other publish error keeps its existing outcome. A new Tier 1 transport fault emits 10158 before commit, and production Start and Signal both advance virtual time by 25 ms, retry, and retain one wakeup in the focused model checks. The 1,000-seed 20-signal pipeline now includes this response among its fault choices, verifies same-ID retry and exact trace replay, and passed locally. The full Tier 1 suite and focused three-node signal tests passed locally. A separate three-node contract started 64 concurrent `Client.Enqueue` calls with one message ID; three repeats returned success to every caller and retained exactly one wakeup through all three nodes. That contract does not prove a 10158 response occurred in those repeats; the clean-runner failures supplied the observed error.

The [first clean-runner 20-seed run with the 10158 retry](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36659839832) passed seeds 1–15, then failed seed 16's terminal p99 at 31.14 seconds. Its ten parents, six children, and 12 grandchildren all completed and passed the retained audit; three timer parents were the slowest at 30.66–31.14 seconds. Worker timer-lateness metrics peaked near 3.5 seconds, but aggregate metrics cannot locate the remaining wait. Failure-only diagnostics now fetch every slow invocation's journal entry timestamps and worker IDs. This is a timer liveness miss, and the broader 20-seed gate remains open.

The [per-push test run at `f8c7fba`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36660257248) exposed a separate verification bottleneck: 500 concurrent same-ID Starts yielded one `started`, 494 `already_started`, and five `unknown` responses, but the Porcupine Start checker returned `Unknown` after its 45-second search budget. A synthetic valid burst with its one success late in the overlapping history reproduced that checker timeout in five seconds. The checker uses a direct interval proof only for uniform same-input, same-ID bursts; an `already_started` return before a separate confirmed call begins or a mismatched invocation sequence still fails. A [later clean-runner job](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36661830289) exposed the other confirmed outcome, `enqueue_unknown`, with 474 `already_started` and 25 `unknown` responses; the fast path initially missed it and Porcupine again timed out. The proof now accepts one `started`, one `enqueue_unknown`, or a burst in which a lost publish acknowledgment makes the earliest `already_started` call self-observe the commit. It matches Porcupine on 448 small overlap and unknown-outcome variants, and the existing Porcupine model handles every other Start history. Ten focused local leader-kill repeats passed after the change, including one burst with 236 `unknown` outcomes; clean-runner validation of the self-observed case remains open.

Two later clean-runner mixed runs passed all 20 seeds and all 28 invocations per seed: [the same-ID concurrency test revision](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36660121242) peaked at 18.50 seconds, and [the seeded 10158 pipeline revision](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36660257160) peaked at 29.84 seconds on seed 19, just under the 30-second gate. These passes do not explain the preceding timer delay or provide much margin on the second run. A [200-seed run on the all-invocation trace revision](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36661143444) is in progress.

The [next 20-seed clean-runner run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36660833320) passed seeds 1–19, then failed seed 20's terminal p99 at 36.28 seconds. Its slow signal workflow suspended at +9.22 seconds from the last committed signal and did not commit another `SignalConsumed` entry until +30.63 seconds, a 21.41-second gap close to the 20-second consumer `AckWait`. The post-heal signal scan had inspected 32 signals and reenqueued 29, but the retained journal and aggregate worker metrics do not show whether a NAK, wakeup, or lease release was delayed. All 28 invocations completed and passed the retained audit; the latency gate remains open.

Another [clean-runner run before the timed retry](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36662298872) failed at seed 9's 31.43-second p99. Its slow signal workflow suspended at +9.65 seconds after consuming thirteen signals and did not consume the next signal until +30.29 seconds, a second 20.64-second gap. The last three signals and final steps then completed by +31.43 seconds. This repeat narrows the observed delay to resumption after a ready suspension; it still does not prove which NATS acknowledgment or wakeup was lost.

The production suspended-wait scanner now scopes its deduplicated wakeup ID to the journal suspension sequence and a ten-second time window. Repeated scans in one window retain one run; a still-ready suspension in the next window gets a fresh run before the 20-second consumer redelivery fallback. The Tier 1 transport model uses the same ID construction, and the seeded suspended-scan workload checks the new-window retry and same-window dedup with virtual time. A separate 1,000-seed transport replay drops a wakeup NAK before commit and proves the fresh scanner run is fetched before the original 20-second redelivery; it checks exact trace replay, terminal no-op handling, and a drained modeled consumer. The full simulator suite, focused three-node scanner contracts, and local replays of CI seeds 9 and 20 passed; their terminal p99 values were 9.74 and 9.16 seconds. Race-instrumented local replays of those seeds also passed at 17.93 and 20.07 seconds. The [first 20-seed clean-runner run with the timed retry](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36663160960) passed all 28 audits per seed with a worst terminal p99 of 24.39 seconds on seed 12. The [100,000-seed Tier 1 run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36664169752) covering the new lost-NAK replay passed at `0531108`: 5,300,603 generated schedules, 151,051,853 choices, and 1,264,244,076 transport events in 51m11.6s of Go test time. It predates the later partial-page read-error fix and dispatch diagnostics, which have focused tests. A [second clean 20-seed run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36663348010) also passed with a worst terminal p99 of 17.72 seconds. These clean runs do not prove the broader release gates.

The [third clean-runner 20-seed run with the timed retry](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36663423689) failed at seed 17 despite complete retained audits. One signal workflow suspended at +9.30 seconds and did not consume its next signal until +30.41 seconds; its terminal latency was 35.24 seconds. A fan-out child did not consume its completion signals until +36.34 seconds after its last grandchild, and its terminal latency was 37.44 seconds. The existing journal trace cannot tell whether the suspended scanner reached either invocation or whether a published wakeup waited in the consumer. The mixed fixture now records each production scanner pass, cursor, ready candidates, reenqueues, and errors on a latency failure. It also requires the durable run queue to drain after all terminal audits, catching leftover retry wakeups. Local seed 9 and 17 replays passed the new queue assertion; the clean-runner latency gate remains open.

The [fourth clean-runner 20-seed pass](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36663798983) succeeded at `0531108`. The [first pass with the scanner trace and queue-drain assertion](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36664668354) succeeded at `27c6cac`: all 20 seeds completed and audited 28 invocations and drained `WF_RUN`, with the slowest terminal p99 at 20.37 seconds on seed 17. A race-instrumented local seed 17 replay also passed the new queue assertion at 23.25 seconds. The earlier seed 17 failure remains unexplained, and the release-count run below found another latency miss.

The [200-seed release-count run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36664161691) at `0531108` passed seeds 1–44 and failed seed 45 at a 34.25-second terminal p99. Two timer invocations had suspended roughly 12.4 seconds before their final deadlines, then both wrote their first due `StepCompleted` entries about 30.25 seconds after those deadlines. All 28 invocations reached terminal journals; the worker metrics showed 602 lease contentions and 620 redeliveries across the two workers. The saved seed 45 fault schedule injected a 100 ms disk delay, a route partition, a server pause, and a server kill. A race-instrumented local seed 45 replay on the newer code passed at 12.80 seconds, and a second local replay with dispatch observation passed at 21.70 seconds; the seed and fault schedule alone do not reproduce the slow server/worker interleaving. The worker now optionally reports per-invocation fetch, lease, retry, and ack events, which the mixed fixture records and prints for slow invocations on a latency failure. This should separate a late delivery from lease contention or execution retries on the next occurrence. The release-count gate remains open.

The suspended scanner now preserves verified ready wakeups when another invocation in the same scan page returns a read error. It leaves the cursor at that page and reports the error, so the failed read is retried while the independent wakeups can already run. An in-memory transport test injects one transient invocation-read timeout at each of three page positions, checks the two unaffected wakeups are published, and checks the retry adds exactly the missed wakeup without duplicating the earlier ones. The focused normal and race tests pass. A matching three-node contract test also passed: the real adapter published two wakeups despite an injected read timeout, then recovered the third on retry without duplicate queue entries. This closes a scanner head-of-line delay in the runtime logic; it does not establish that such a timeout caused the earlier seed 17 latency failure.

A [20-seed clean-runner run with that scanner change](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36666014226) failed seed 9 at 31.85-second terminal p99. Its slow signal invocation consumed thirteen signals by +9.53 seconds after the final committed signal, then suspended at +9.96 and did not consume the remaining three until +30.57. The recorded suspended scanner had no errors: it identified this invocation and completed an enqueue attempt at +13.40, +17.17, +21.12, +25.24, +29.18, and +33.14 seconds. Same-window message-ID deduplication can collapse some attempts. This rules out a missed scanner candidate in that run, but the trace has no per-invocation worker fetch or lease timing, so it cannot yet distinguish delayed delivery from lease contention or a failed execution. The new dispatch observer above captures those points on later runs. The three-node dropped-NAK contract and Tier 1 replay already deliver a distinct handoff run before the old message's `AckWait` on a healthy consumer; this real fault-run miss remains open.

The [targeted clean-runner seeds 41–60 run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36666900570) with the dispatch observer failed seed 55 at a 34.63-second terminal p99. The slow signal invocation's worker acquired its lease at −0.65 seconds relative to the final signal, consumed ten signals, and then reported an execution retry after suspending at +9.59 seconds. Both workers fetched fresh and redelivered run messages for that invocation but repeatedly received `ErrHeld` until a worker finally acquired the lease at +30.54 seconds; the remaining six signals and terminal steps then completed by +34.63. This identifies a retained lease after worker cancellation as the immediate cause of this miss, rather than absent scanner wakeups or a consumer that never fetched them. The observer did not record the release and cleanup result, so the reason that lease remained held is still unconfirmed. Release and cleanup attempts now emit bounded per-delivery events on a latency failure. A race-instrumented local seed 55 replay passed at 9.33 seconds, so the fault schedule alone still does not reproduce the slow interleaving. The under-30-second gate remains open.

A pinned Tier 1 trace now reproduces the retained-lease portion of that failure under explicit modeled replies: the old owner renews, its release delete is dropped before commit, and its cleanup read loses transport. Production lease calls keep the replacement fenced until the renewed TTL, then a higher-epoch replacement completes a four-entry journal while stale cleanup, renewal, and append are rejected. This is a candidate explanation for the lease remaining held, not a claim that these exact server replies occurred in seed 55. The trace uses the current 12-second TTL; the original real failure ran at 20 seconds.

A focused three-node lease-expiry race found a separate adapter mismatch visible in the high-contention mixed logs. Of 32 simultaneous acquirers after a short-TTL key expired, one won, 21 received `ErrHeld`, and ten received raw JetStream CAS error 10164. The local nats.go `Create` path can expose that response when contenders race to replace an expired delete marker. The production KV adapter now normalizes this specific Create conflict to `ErrKeyExists`, preserving the underlying error; the existing lease decision then returns `ErrHeld`. Three real-cluster repeats and a race run passed with one higher-epoch winner and 31 held losers. The in-memory lease transport already modeled the normalized outcome. This removes an avoidable one-second generic-error retry in that race; it does not establish how much of the earlier mixed p99 delay came from these responses.

The matching Tier 1 workload now cooperatively schedules 32 production acquirers after lease expiry. Its 1,000-seed default gate requires one higher-epoch winner, 31 `ErrHeld` losers, and rejection of the expired holder's renewal and cleanup without changing the successor. The first ten seeds replay exactly; seed 42 is pinned and byte-identical across processes. Normal and race runs passed. A local 100,000-seed run of this workload also passed in 65.0 seconds, with 6,400,000 scheduler choices and 7,000,000 transport events. The model checks the normalized KV contract; it does not reproduce NATS delete-marker internals or replace the real adapter contract.

A following [targeted seeds 51–70 run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36667929659) with release and cleanup events passed all 20 seeds; seed 55 measured 17.58 seconds and the slowest seed measured 18.08 seconds. It did not reproduce a release failure. To reduce the worst-case lease-expiry wait exposed by seed 55, the default `WF_LEASE` TTL is now 12 seconds and the renewal heartbeat is three seconds. The 20-second consumer `AckWait` remains unchanged. This bounds takeover sooner when a lease remains held, but does not explain why the observed lease was retained. Provisioning still rejects an existing bucket with a different TTL; operators must stop lease holders and explicitly update an existing 20-second bucket before this version starts. The local five-container SIGKILL and 45-second pause tests passed with one terminal journal and stale-writer fencing; successor completion took 20.02 and 20.01 seconds respectively after the fault, limited by the unchanged delivery wait. The [clean five-container worker recovery run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36669477073) passed at `6535106`: kill-to-terminal was 20.005 seconds, pause-to-successor-terminal was 20.004 seconds, and the stale worker was fenced with one immutable terminal journal. A local mixed seed 55 replay passed its retained audit with a 9.95-second terminal p99 across 28 invocations. The [clean 20-seed mixed run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36669467067) passed all audits and its slowest terminal p99 was 27.02 seconds at seed 11; the [full per-push suite](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36669467071) passed. The [clean 200-seed mixed run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36669476874) at this TTL later failed seed 83, while the [100,000-seed Tier 1 run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36669502418) passed; detailed outcomes are recorded below. The broader gates remain open.

A [later clean 20-seed mixed run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36670195605) failed seed 14 with a 37.68-second terminal p99 despite complete retained audits. The slow signal invocation acquired its lease 0.58 seconds after the final signal, stayed on the same worker until it completed at +36.42 seconds, and released the lease successfully. It journaled all 16 signals and then 16 awaited-signal step outcomes sequentially; this was a processing-throughput miss, not a delayed initial wakeup or retained lease. Meanwhile its two workers recorded 1,144 lease contentions and 1,244 redeliveries across the fixture, with many other run messages for the active invocation nacked every second. The held-lease NAK delay is now five seconds to reduce those retries while keeping each run recoverable. In one local seed 14 replay, contentions fell from 271 to 59 and redeliveries from 270 to 67, while the terminal p99 was 16.31 seconds; different real interleavings prevent treating that pair as a controlled throughput benchmark. Local seed 55 also passed at 8.95 seconds. The held-lease timer redelivery test passed with the new delay. A clean-runner release-count result for the change is still required.

The [clean-runner seeds 41–60 run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36671703928) with the five-second delay passed all 20 seeds and 28 retained audits per seed. Seed 55 measured 8.99 seconds and the slowest terminal p99 was 17.76 seconds at seed 58. This range includes earlier failure seeds 45 and 55 but does not replace the 200-consecutive-seed release-count run.

The [regular seeds 1–20 run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36671683534) at the five-second backoff also passed, with a worst terminal p99 of 24.94 seconds. The [200-seed run at that backoff](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36671986890) passed seeds 1–36 and failed seed 37 at 51.55 seconds despite complete retained terminal audits. Its slowest signal invocation acquired at +4.59 seconds and released successfully at +51.64 seconds; timer and grandchild traces also show renewal deadlines, fenced cleanup, and waits for retained leases. Raw Create CAS errors 10164 appear in the trace; this run predates their adapter normalization. The [earlier 200-seed run with the 12-second TTL and one-second backoff](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36669476874) passed seeds 1–82 and failed seed 83 at 73.82 seconds. Neither run satisfies the release-count gate, and these observations do not establish a server-side cause.

The [100,000-seed Tier 1 run at the 12-second TTL](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36669502418) passed: 5,300,603 generated schedules, 151,051,853 scheduler choices, and 1,264,244,076 transport events in 46m39.9s. It predates the canceled-worker retained-lease trace, five-second backoff, and 32-contender expiry workload. The newer extended run and the 200-seed cluster run with CAS normalization remain pending.

The [per-push chaos smoke at the five-second backoff](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36671683522) passed the four-fault short and timer cells, then its single-signal cell failed while constructing the replacement worker: the bounded `WF_STATE` bucket lookup returned `context deadline exceeded` shortly after route healing. The mixed fixture already retries this constructor during recovery. The single-workflow fixture now also retries it for at most 30 seconds, keeping each attempt bounded to five seconds. One local seed 42 signal replay passed with a 25.66-second start-to-result time. This addresses the fixture's recovery race; the precise server-side cause of that timed-out lookup remains unconfirmed.

Two consecutive per-push combined-rebalance jobs, [before](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36671165113) and [after](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36672802477) the held-lease NAK backoff, read all 200 workflow results but hit the six-minute test context at the run-queue drain check. The old failure printed only `run.Info` with that expired context, so it cannot distinguish queued messages from an unavailable final stream-info response. The failure path now uses a fresh ten-second context to report the run stream state, pending and ack-pending counts for all four busy durable consumers, and their assignment owners. The six-minute gate and requirement for a drained queue remain unchanged; the cause is still open.

The [per-push 500-child fan-out job at CAS normalization](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36673286642) passed the ordinary and parent-SIGKILL cells, but the journal-leader-restart cell exhausted its five-minute context while opening a filtered journal consumer. The last logged progress was the leader restart after 382 child requests. A following run at `61401ff` passed that cell, so the older failure remains unexplained. The fixture now retains the latest 256 replacement-parent dispatch events and, on a creation-phase read failure or timeout, reports its metrics, journal state and parent tail through all three nodes, and the parent durable consumer with a fresh ten-second diagnostic context. This preserves the original failure gate and should distinguish parent dispatch failure from an observer read failure on the next occurrence.

A local leader-restart reproduction with those diagnostics failed in 302.95 seconds. Its parent had reached suspension and acknowledged its run within seconds; all three nodes agreed on the parent's tail at index 1014, and its durable consumer had zero pending and ack-pending messages. The observer had not completed its first post-restart journal read. The batch read loop could repeatedly fetch no entries while its direct probe found the next entry, without replacing the cursor or bounding that loop. It now replaces a cursor after two empty pulls, preserving the last verified sequence, and returns a timeout after six consecutive empty pulls with no progress. A separate 1,000-seed Tier 1 workload covers transient and permanent empty pulls before and after partial delivery, checks cursor lifecycle and no skipped entries, and fails against the former implementation. Seed 42 is pinned and byte-identical across processes. A local 100,000-seed run of the new workload passed in 39.46 seconds with 24,022,862 transport events. The full `sim` and `journal` suites and focused race tests passed; three real leader-restart fan-out runs passed after the change in 10.44, 17.08, and 10.84 seconds with complete retained audits. The exact server behavior behind the stalled cursor remains unconfirmed, and fresh CI validation is pending.

The [per-push suite with the cursor replacement](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36675741070) passed. The [200-seed mixed run with lease CAS normalization](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36673323971) passed seeds 1–64 and failed seed 65 at a 53.08-second terminal p99. The release-count gate remains open.

The first sustained Tier 2 matrix row now runs the 40/30/20/10 parent mix continuously in repeated batches on one three-process cluster, kills the current `WF_JRN` leader every 30 seconds, and verifies each restart's replica catch-up. Its default duration is ten minutes; each batch includes six children and 12 grandchildren, producing 28 retained invocations. It records Start, Signal, and Await histories plus worker dispatch events and actual fault times, checks retained state every ten batches and at the final cut, requires each workload's terminal p99 below 30 seconds, checks the final-heal completion deadline, and requires a drained run queue. A manual `tier2-matrix-journal` workflow supports 1, 20, or 200 consecutive seeds with separate artifacts. Two shortened local runs passed with 196 terminal invocations and one leader kill; the first aggregate p99 was 19.99 seconds and the second passed all six per-type gates. Both explicitly report `release_duration=false` and do not count as ten-minute evidence. A further shortened run with the race detector passed all per-type gates and the retained audit in 68.46 seconds of test time.

The first ten-minute attempt was intentionally terminated for stack capture after its batch-20 checkpoint stopped reporting progress. The stack showed the invariant checker waiting in a raw journal `GetMsg` request with the full sixteen-minute fixture context, rather than a blocked workflow handler. Checkpoint audits now use twenty-second attempts and at most three fresh-context retries for named transient transport errors; invariant errors fail immediately. Individual final invocation audits are also bounded. The interrupted run is not a completed matrix result. The fresh ten-minute local run completed 52 batches and 19 leader kills, then failed in the signal history model because its global two-minute history-span guard rejected the sustained run. The [first clean-runner full-duration row](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36678021922) completed its workload but failed the signal model on two generic `context deadline exceeded` outcomes from five-second attempts before publication. The SDK observer now records `not_published` only when a generic error occurs before `PublishSignal`; the checker validates a zero signal sequence and leaves its queue state unchanged. Post-publication failures retain their previous classification. A production-client port test verifies the recorded deadline outcome, and checker tests reject a claimed sequence for an unpublished attempt. The remaining matrix rows, 200 clean full-matrix seeds, and Tier 3 soak remain open.

An opt-in Linux process-cluster test now suspends 1,000 native timers, kills and restarts all three NATS server processes before their due times, and checks every retained schedule, result, due-time boundary, journal, and the drained run queue. The first local attempt caught a fixture error: future scheduled sources remain counted in `WF_RUN`, so a pre-restart count of zero was incorrect. With that assertion corrected, the local 90-second-delay run passed in 109.13 seconds. A second run with a 150-second due-time margin passed in 162.46 seconds and reported 1,000 invocations, 1,000 journals, 5,000 entries, and 1,000 terminal results. The [manual `timer-1000-restart` CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36581508945) passed on a clean runner in 170.61 seconds with the same retained-state counts.

A regular three-node timer test now forces a scheduled wakeup to arrive while a signal-resumed handler holds the invocation lease inside a blocked effect. A second worker must nack the wakeup with delay and observe its redelivery; after the effect releases, the timer completes from a later delivery. The test requires one effect execution, one timer await completion, one terminal journal, a drained run queue, and a passing raw-state audit. Three repeated local runs and one race run passed. This covers the held-lease timer interleaving in the Phase 5 edge cases; it is not a thousands-due-in-one-second throughput result.

An opt-in three-node fan-in proof now starts 3,000 workflows that journal `wf.Now` before deriving a replay-stable duration to one shared deadline. The full local run placed all 3,000 journaled `fire_at` times in one UTC second with a 212.99 ms spread. All results and journals completed; p99 handler lateness was 3.09 seconds, maximum 3.13 seconds, and the 3.19-second first-due-to-last-completion window observed 940.1 completions/s. The largest partition held 52 timers while its durable consumer allowed 1,000 pending acknowledgments, so that configured limit did not bind this run. The raw-state report was 3,000 invocations, 3,000 journals, 21,000 entries, and 3,000 terminal results. The [manual `timer-fanin-3000` CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36588937157) passed on a clean runner: 165.64 ms due-time spread, 2.34-second p99 lateness, 2.36-second delivery window, and 1,269.5 observed completions/s with the same retained-state counts. These are observed rates at one workload and worker configuration, not a measured saturation ceiling.

The larger local 10,000-timer fan-in run also placed every journaled deadline in one UTC second, with a 663.22 ms spread. All 10,000 results completed, and the raw-state checker found 10,000 invocations, 10,000 journals, 70,000 entries, and 10,000 terminal results. The p99 handler lateness was 10.79 seconds and the 10.87-second delivery window observed 920.3 completions/s; the busiest partition held 162 timers, below its 1,000-message `MaxAckPending` limit. Together with the local 3,000-timer rate of 940.1/s, this suggests the six-worker, 32-per-partition local configuration levels near 900–950 completions/s for these bursts, but does not establish a universal throughput ceiling. The [manual `timer-fanin-10000` CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36590273938) passed on a clean runner: 255.61 ms due-time spread, 9.10-second p99 lateness, 9.14-second delivery window, and 1,093.9 observed completions/s with the same 70,000-entry retained-state audit.

The Phase 4 unsupported-goroutine edge now has a controlled replay test: two goroutines issue distinct steps in one order, replay succeeds when that order is repeated, and replay fails with `ErrNonDeterministic` when the scheduling order is reversed. Barriers serialize access to the workflow context so the test checks journal ordering rather than an unsynchronized data race. Twenty normal and ten race-instrumented repetitions passed.

A CI run at `9a23a73` failed the 10,000-round journal CAS race at round 505, after the first leader restart: one writer received a wrong-last-sequence reply while its subject-tail read stayed at 505 through three attempts. The server-side cause remains unconfirmed. The runtime now permits 40 bounded same-CAS attempts (up to 975 ms of waits), and the seeded model checks recovery after four unchanged-tail rejections and `ErrUnknown` after 40. The pre-change 550-round leader-restart test passed ten local repetitions; after the change, ten more 550-round runs and one full 10,000-round run with 20 leader restarts passed. Additional full runs are needed to establish whether the rare real failure is resolved.

The cluster CI runs at `6870bcf` and `b355ac1` later returned `ErrUnknown` with a context deadline exceeded from one CAS writer at rounds 4,131 and 5,247. Those logs did not capture the retained tail, so they cannot distinguish a committed publish with a lost response from an absent publish. The 10,000-round test now rereads the retained subject after an unknown reply, requires exactly one next entry with the expected index and writer, and continues the final contiguous-journal audit; rounds without a physical winner still fail. It reports unknown-round counts separately from normal one-success/one-stale rounds. A 1,000-seed cooperative two-writer workload models both a dropped publish and a hidden committed acknowledgment; every schedule retains one next journal entry and the expected caller outcomes. A real hidden-ack fixture exercised the retained-read resolution path, and one local 10,000-round run with 20 leader restarts passed with zero unknown rounds. The cause of the CI timeouts remains unconfirmed.

The `196bec6` CAS scale CI job completed its rounds but timed out creating the ordered consumer for the final 10,001-entry audit. The audit now tries bounded consumer creation through all three replicas, logging each failed peer and still requiring the complete ordered entry and sequence audit. Local 1,000- and 10,000-round runs passed after this change; the latter completed 20 leader restarts and read all 10,001 entries in 303 ms. The cause of the CI consumer-creation stall remains unconfirmed.

A later cluster CI run at `37e1033` stopped round 9,001 before the CAS publish barrier: a fresh `WF_JRN` stream-handle lookup returned a context deadline to one writer. That result did not exercise a server CAS race, and the lookup timeout cause remains unconfirmed. The race fixture now reuses stream handles across rounds and refreshes them after each leader restart; a writer retries up to three `ErrUnknown` tail lookups only when it has not reached the publish barrier. A three-node injected tail-lookup fixture passed three repeats, a 550-round leader-restart run passed, and a full 10,000-round run passed with 20 leader restarts and zero unknown rounds. A 1,000-seed cooperative two-writer workload injects the same pre-publish lookup loss and checks one success, one stale outcome, and one retained next entry.

The `d95d9f5`, `23a1a50`, `ee5b581`, and `7730382` cluster CI jobs failed because an injected-rejection contract still expected `ErrUnknown` after three replies, the old retry limit. The real-adapter contract now checks success after four unchanged-tail replies and `ErrUnknown` after 40; three race-instrumented local repeats passed. The first CI workflow with the corrected contract, `303978b`, passed its cluster and unit jobs. The earlier failures do not establish a new server discrepancy.

The cluster CI run at `464d23b` later timed out in `TestProvisionRejectsJournalPerSubjectCap` while changing the real `WF_JRN` stream configuration. The failed run did not reread the stream, so the update's commit outcome is unknown. The test now uses bounded update attempts and confirms the altered cap from two nodes before asking `provision.Ensure` to reject it. Ten pre-change and ten post-change local repeats passed, and the later `da2a362` and `b3c476b` cluster CI runs passed; the original timeout cause remains unconfirmed.

The cluster CI run at `9bfe0bb` failed the 30-day timer retention test because a `WF_RUN` target message remained before the first restart. The old assertion treated any target message as an early timer delivery, even though the initial start message uses the same subject; one of ten pre-change local repeats reproduced it. The test now waits for that start message to drain and distinguishes an early scheduled target by its timer headers. One focused run and ten repeated three-node runs passed after the change. The failed log did not retain the message headers, so its precise message identity remains unconfirmed.

The `1a60a5d` cluster CI run later returned no rows from the migrated search-attribute index immediately after `Rebuild` on a client pinned to another replica. Ten focused reruns passed, so the cause is unconfirmed. The test now waits up to five seconds for the new index to become readable without rerunning `Rebuild`; if it stays absent, it reports the direct row and invocation stream info to distinguish replica read lag from a missed rebuild. The `7402121` full cluster rerun passed; the earlier readback timeout cause remains unconfirmed.

The seeded client-to-scanner-to-worker signal pipeline now sends each worker `SignalConsumed` append through production `journal.Store.Append` and the same in-memory stream model used by journal fault tests. Each seed loses one committed journal acknowledgment at a chosen signal, reloads the retained journal as a redelivered worker would, and drains the rest. It compares every retained stream sequence and payload with the records used for consumed-signal retry and worker replay.

The retained-state integrity checker now accepts a modeled snapshot through the same journal validation used for real JetStream. Negative controls deliberately duplicate an invocation (I1), assign two workers one epoch or descend an epoch (I2), record a completion without a request (I3), and change a terminal KV value (I6); each is rejected. The real checker now rejects two nonempty worker IDs recorded under one nonzero epoch. A 1,000-seed workload runs production start, journal append, and worker terminal-persistence decisions, reconstructs retained invocation/journal/KV state after each of five modeled completions per seed, and checks I1/I2/I3/I6 with exact trace replay. Another 1,000-seed workload journals three production `wf.Run` steps per invocation, replays their retained requests without rerunning effects, and verifies changed step names and inputs separately fail the I4 determinism guard. Retained-state I5 checks now verify suspended timer/signal waits and eligible committed signals after virtual time and faults heal; they name blocked waits and reject missing repair wakeups. Negative controls catch skipped scanners, dropped publishes, and removed retained messages. A separate 1,000-seed outcome workload covers ambiguous KV create/update replies, tombstone replacement, and terminal immutability. A 1,000-seed production tombstone sweep workload covers KV key enumeration, expiry, old and reused invocation generations, dry run, changed KV revision, dropped delete, lost delete acknowledgment, and an idempotent second pass; a complete-sweep three-node differential contract passed three repeats and a race run. A separate 1,000-seed production blob sweep workload models stream holes, shared and snapshot object references, young objects, uncertain deletes, and missing or corrupt snapshot reads; a three-node full-sweep differential contract passed three repeats and a race run. Its retained-reference purges are fixture actions, not production `retention.Purge` stages. A new 1,000-seed combined workload runs production `retention.PurgeWithPort` and blob sweeping on shared modeled state, faults marker, signal, journal, timer, snapshot, tombstone, purge-event, and invocation stages, and verifies idempotent recovery plus final reclamation; a three-node clean-path differential contract passed three repeats and a race run. The combined model now runs production `journal.Store.SnapshotPrefix` to write the snapshot object and manifest and purge the covered prefix through the same retained transport before production `journal.Store.Read` reconstructs the compacted prefix and live terminal suffix. Its three-node contract runs the same production snapshot write on real and modeled stores, then verifies that corrupt snapshot bytes stop purge before its marker and that repair permits retry. A 1,000-seed cooperative schedule now interleaves production snapshot transport calls with retention purge while a modeled worker holds its lease, then releases it and reclaims blobs after purge. A three-node fixture blocks a real snapshot upload, confirms purge returns `ErrActive`, then verifies reconstruction and reclamation after release. A further 1,000-seed schedule runs production journal `Append` concurrently with production `SnapshotPrefix` on the same retained transport, then runs purge and blob sweeping after the worker lease releases. Both snapshot cutoffs preserve the later terminal append. A dropped append request and a committed append with a hidden acknowledgment are resolved by a production journal read; only the absent entry is retried. A three-node fixture blocks snapshot upload and verifies all three append outcomes, the fixed purge bound, and full reconstruction. A 1,000-seed cooperative schedule now runs the production worker handler and an independent compactor against the same modeled journal, with dropped and hidden-ack snapshot object, manifest, and purge writes. It verifies 32 effects execute once, the handler completes during compaction, a later compaction repairs uncertain writes, and production read reconstructs all 66 entries from the snapshot plus four live entries. Online blob sweeping remains open; sweeping still requires quiescent writers. A transient state read after the invocation vanished previously returned `ErrNotFound`; it now returns the transport error so a retry can finish. A short-handler workload now runs these production decisions together; native timer delivery is now modeled in a separate integrated workload; a two-compactor snapshot race is modeled separately. Running cancellation, heartbeat handoff, large result objects, and snapshot read/write faults now have separate modeled workloads; online blob-sweep and concurrent heartbeat/failure actor schedules remain open.

Tier 1 CI now replays fifty pinned traces for ambiguous CAS replies, two-worker dispatch, competing suspended scanners, signal and suspended wakeup liveness, child notification, outcome persistence, integrated worker execution, signal resume, running cancellation, worker heartbeat and handoff, native timer wakeup, fallback timer wakeup, timer/signal select, integrated child completion, large result objects, compacted snapshot reads, snapshot write recovery, concurrent compaction, and worker-triggered compaction, retained-state checks, and workflow determinism. Two tombstone sweep traces pin a lost KV delete acknowledgment and a concurrent state replacement; two blob sweep traces pin a lost object delete reply and an unavailable snapshot read. Five combined purge/blob traces pin lost purge-event and invocation-purge replies, a transient state read after the invocation disappeared, a one-read snapshot visibility delay, and corrupt snapshot bytes. Two snapshot/purge lease traces pin a fenced purge and a purge after worker release. Three append/snapshot/purge traces pin both retained snapshot cutoffs, a dropped append, and a hidden committed acknowledgment. One CAS trace pins a transient tail lookup before publish and safe two-writer retry. One worker/compactor trace pins a dropped purge during handler execution and replays byte-identically across processes. Two skewed lease traces pin both sides of the one-second orphan-reclaim boundary with distinct actor wall-clock offsets; server-clock KV expiry remains shared. A three-node contract compares real and modeled slow/fast clock decisions on one uninitialized lease; three repeats and a race run passed. The per-push seeded loops remain at 1,000 each; `SIM_SEEDS` now raises every loop together, and a local 10,000-per-workload run passed in 334.5 seconds of Go test time on the expanded four-CPU VM. A manual `tier1-extended` CI workflow can measure 10,000 or run 100,000 seeds per workload and retains the same failure-trace artifact. The first 10,000-seed-per-workload GitHub Actions run passed at `77fac0d` in 378.9 seconds of Go test time (381.8 seconds wall), beyond the plan's few-minute condition for raising that per-workload push gate. The default 1,000-seed-per-workload run already generates about 49,600 schedules in aggregate per push. The opt-in coverage summary reports model version, schedule count, scheduler choices per second, transport events, and virtual-time buckets; a local 1,000-seed run counted 49,602 generated schedules and 1,503,118 choices in 34.1 seconds. Go runs the `sim` package from its own directory, so the relative `sim-failure.json` path matches the CI artifact glob. The mistaken `sim/` prefix introduced at `27a4d1e` has been removed.

The second 10,000-seed-per-workload GitHub Actions run passed at `ecbf4de`: 490,602 generated schedules, 15,013,622 scheduler choices, and 107,283,068 modeled transport events in 403.973 seconds of Go test time (407.01 seconds wall). It exercised the opt-in coverage summary in CI.

The first 100,000-seed-per-workload GitHub Actions run finished in 64 minutes and found one worker/compactor assertion failure at seed 11508 after about 4.8 million schedules. The saved trace showed a lost purge acknowledgment reached the worker before the independent compactor; the worker recovered it and the compactor returned success. The assertion now checks that exactly one injected fault was exercised and verifies the final retained state regardless of which actor reached the shared snapshot port first. Seed 11508 is pinned in the regression corpus. The rerun at `90d06b7` passed 100,000 seeds per workload: 4,900,602 generated schedules, 150,114,434 scheduler choices, and 1,073,544,741 modeled transport events in 45m56.8s of Go test time. This clears the Tier 1 seed-count gate for the implemented model slices; the model does not yet cover every planned transport edge.
