A second 100,000-seed-per-workload [CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36552238318) passed at `c1c6a83` after adding the dropped-NAK heartbeat-handoff mode. Model version 3 recorded 4,900,602 generated schedules, 150,114,434 choices, and 1,075,094,711 transport events in 1h6m43.6s of Go test time. The extra run validates the newer modeled path at the release seed count; it does not extend the model to the still-open transport edges.

The `7402121` chaos job passed all 20 four-fault stream seeds and completed the short production workflow with result `42`, then failed its retained-journal audit while the third server was still killed. That audit is now performed after restarting the third server; the test still proves completion on the two-node majority before restart and requires the restarted node to serve the immutable result. Short, native-timer, and signal variants passed locally after the change; the `90d06b7` chaos-smoke CI job passed all 20 stream seeds and all three workflow variants. Its full cluster job remains in progress. The majority-side journal read timeout is still an unconfirmed server-side observation.

A four-fault fan-out workflow now starts six asynchronous children before quorum loss, then resumes their worker partitions after route healing and leader resumption. The parent must return the sum `42` on the surviving majority, the restarted third node must serve the same result and each child result, and the final retained-state checker must find seven distinct terminal invocations and journals. Four focused local runs and one race-instrumented run passed. The per-push chaos job now exercises this fourth workload after short, timer, and signal variants. This is one real-cluster matrix slice, not the 40/30/20/10 mixed generator or 200-seed Tier 2 gate.

The regular 500-child fan-out test now has a second variant that kills and restarts the actual `WF_JRN` leader after a seeded prefix of child requests is committed and the first parent worker stops. It waits for a different journal leader and the restarted replica to catch up before resuming the parent, then verifies the parent sum, all 500 distinct child invocations, and 501 terminal journals. Local seeds 1, 2, and 42 passed with the leader cut after 382, 387, and 106 child requests respectively. This covers one leader-fault slice of the 500-child matrix; the other server and worker faults remain open.

A third regular 500-child variant runs the first parent worker in a separate process and sends it a real `SIGKILL` after a seeded child-request prefix. Before killing it, the parent test verifies the retained journal has exactly the committed request/completion pairs. A successor replays the prefix, creates the remaining children, and the same final audit requires the parent sum, 500 distinct child invocations, and 501 terminal journals. Local seeds 1, 2, and 42 passed after process kills at 382, 387, and 106 committed children; both existing variants also passed after sharing the handler fixture. This directly exercises the plan's parent-worker kill point, while broader 500-child server and network faults remain open.

Twenty consecutive local parent-`SIGKILL` seeds (1–20) then passed on the final replicated-read fixture. Their cuts ranged from 110 to 387 committed child requests; each run used a fresh three-node cluster and checked all 501 terminal invocations and journals. The [per-push suite at `a169809`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36560259128) passed with the new process-kill variant, and the [follow-up suite at `62beeac`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36560415114) passed with the pre-kill replicated-read wait.

The opt-in full-server-restart fan-out test now also runs at 500 children on three real NATS processes. It waits until all child requests and invocations are retained, `SIGKILL`s all three servers, restarts them on the same file stores, runs successor workers, then verifies the parent sum, every child result, and 501 terminal invocations and journals. The first 500-child attempt reached the results but its raw-state audit timed out after three seconds while scanning 501 invocations; the larger variant now gives that audit up to one minute per attempt. Two full 500-child reruns passed in 62.07 and 37.99 seconds, and the original six-child process-restart test passed after the parameterization. A manual `fanout-500-restart` workflow runs the large proof on CI. This covers one full-cluster-restart slice of the 500-child fault matrix, not the whole matrix.

The first [manual 500-child full-restart CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36562732671) passed at `4ed2feb` in 30.03 seconds of Go test time. Its raw-state audit reported 501 invocations, 501 journals, 4,504 entries, and 501 terminals after the three process restarts.

Worker metrics now record six bounded enqueue-to-lease latency buckets alongside the existing timer lateness buckets. `worker.AggregateMetrics` sums live worker snapshots, and `worker.MetricsHandler` emits process-level counters and cumulative Prometheus latency histograms on each HTTP scrape. A focused export test checks cross-worker aggregation and bucket boundaries; the real three-node lease-contention metrics test checks that every acquired delivery contributes one bucket sample. The new `cmd/wf-worker` process mounts the handler at `/metrics`; live one-node static and KV assignment smoke tests complete a workflow and scrape its counters, including under the race detector. The process also runs the leader-elected tombstone sweep alongside start, signal, timer, and suspended repair loops. A live one-node test starts the runner while NATS is down, restarts that server, then completes a workflow; three repeated normal runs and one race run passed. Startup retries are bounded to 30 seconds and permanent configuration errors still fail immediately. An optional `-retention-type` registers the existing durable purge handler with the process JetStream connection. Live static and KV runner tests now start that workflow, observe `ErrPurged` for the target, and reuse the same ID with a higher invocation sequence; three normal repetitions and one race run passed. A separate one-node runner test preprovisions fallback scheduling, waits for a timed workflow to finish through the process poller, and verifies `WF_TIMER` drains; three normal repetitions and one race run passed. The runner now accepts an exact journal byte cap and serves current `WF_JRN` bytes, limit, and capped utilization ratio with its worker metrics; a live smoke test fills the journal past 70% and checks the scrape. A Prometheus warning rule is provided; receiver routing remains deployment work. An opt-in live runner soak now exercises workflows and scrapes metrics for a configurable 15 or 60 minutes, requiring successful scrapes, monotonic lease counters, journal-byte samples, and clean shutdown. The 15-second local development run completed 43 workflows and 43 scrapes. The [15-minute manual CI soak](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36596403332) passed with 2,551 completed workflows, 2,551 successful scrapes, and 2,551 final lease acquisitions. The [60-minute CI soak](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36599891711) also passed with 10,197 completed workflows, 10,197 successful scrapes, and 10,197 final lease acquisitions. Embedded deployments still need to mount the handler themselves, and those counters reset when Worker instances are replaced.

The Phase 4 SDK property test now generates 10,000 seeded workflow DAGs with journaled steps, zero-duration sleeps, child promises that resolve immediately, and steps that can depend on earlier promise results. It compares each clean result with an independent arithmetic oracle, then injects one append-boundary kill per DAG and requires the resumed result, exact step journal, and distinct child IDs to match the clean run. The first 100 DAGs exercise every append boundary. Normal and race-instrumented runs passed. This is an in-memory SDK appender test of replay decisions, not a live NATS process-kill or transport-fault proof.

An effect that returns a channel, function, or cyclic value now retains a typed `StepCompleted` serialization error, which a retry replays without executing the effect again. Unit tests cover all three values and reject unknown error kinds; a live three-node worker test found a single effect execution, that completion, and a terminal `Failed` record with a passing raw-state audit. The value does not exist until the effect returns, so the plan's request to reject an unserializable *result* before the effect runs is not achievable with the current `Run(ctx, fn)` API. If the completion append itself fails, the usual at-least-once effect rule still applies; inputs remain serializability-checked before the request append and effect.

A journal-limit failure now retains a rejected suspension, panic attempt, or signal drain alongside the existing attempted step request. Offline replay verifies the reproduced handler panic or wait; for a rejected signal drain it exports the retained `WF_SIG` message and checks the attempted sequence, subject, generation, payload, hash, and prior suspended state. Three focused worker and CLI replay runs, race runs of each, and both complete package suites passed. Older failures lacking attempted-entry metadata cannot be verified exactly and fail with an explicit explanation. A rejected signal drain can be exported only while its source signal and any referenced object remain retained.

Worker panic attempts and offline replay now share the same 4 KiB error-text normalization, including a UTF-8 rune cut by that byte limit. A long-panic plugin fixture checks both a normal terminal failure and a journal-capacity failure; both replay without a false mismatch against the retained truncated error.

The per-push cluster run at `5ff8426` failed only in the concurrent-start leader-kill test: all 500 callers returned `ErrAlreadyStarted` after one invocation committed. The client can lose the winning publish acknowledgment and then read its own committed row, which is a valid `ErrAlreadyStarted` outcome under the start history model. The test now accepts zero or one caller with a confirmed start response and still requires 500 recognized outcomes, a legal history, exactly one retained invocation, and one repaired run message. Five local leader-kill repetitions passed after the assertion change.

At `196bec6`, the same leader-kill test reported three `ErrStartUnknown` results after a CAS rejection and a bounded read deadline. That is an explicitly modeled outcome while the leader changes; the assertion now counts it without converting it to success, and a matching `Start` retry after healing must resolve to the one retained invocation sequence. The start history, one-invocation audit, and repaired run-message audit remain required. Three local repeated runs passed; the exact cause of those three read deadlines is unconfirmed.

The opt-in 1,000-timer cancellation proof passed locally on `2251efd` in 175.03 seconds. Four partitions each signaled cancellation near the journaled deadline, then required a terminal `true` result and a cancellation timestamp before `fire_at`. Worker metrics reported 1,000 scheduled timers, zero fired timers, and 1,000 cancelled late wakeups acknowledged as no-ops; the retained-state integrity check also passed. This covers the specified cancellation scale and timing, not the 30-day server-clock-advance proof.

The dedicated [manual 1,000-timer cancellation CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36566632841) passed on `089d060` in 175.09 seconds of Go test time, with the same 1,000 scheduled, zero fired, and 1,000 late no-op counts. The new `timer-cancel-1000` workflow makes this full proof repeatable on a clean runner.

A new full three-process server restart test covers ordered signals across the outage. It suspends a workflow awaiting 100 `go` signals, commits the first 50 with its worker stopped, SIGKILLs and restarts all three NATS processes on the same stores, verifies those 50 remain in `WF_SIG`, commits the next 50, and resumes the worker. The handler and journal both require values 0–99 in order with exactly 100 `SignalConsumed` records and one terminal result; the run queue drains and the raw-state integrity audit passes. Three consecutive local runs and one race-instrumented run passed after stream-leader readiness and same-key retries were added for uncertain post-restart signal responses; one further run passed after the queue-drain check. The per-push chaos smoke job now includes this test. This covers the signal-heavy full-restart cell, not the whole matrix.

The real Start adapter now caches the `WF_INV` stream handle per SDK client after its first successful lookup. This removes repeated stream metadata requests from the duplicate-start confirmation path without caching invocation records, so purge and ID reuse still read current state; the seeded Start transport decisions are unchanged. Five local 500-caller leader-kill repeats passed with exactly three successful handle lookups across three clients, a legal Start history, one retained invocation, and a matching retry after healing. One repeat still returned 126 `ErrStartUnknown` outcomes under the cut, so caching the handle does not establish a latency fix for the confirmation reads. Focused lost-ack, transient-read, and purge/reuse integration tests also passed.

A second process-cluster restart test covers 1,000 short workflows across all 64 dispatch partitions. It SIGKILLs all three server processes with at least 32 handlers inside a held `wf.Run` effect, stops the old worker, restarts the file-backed servers, and runs a successor worker. Every input produces its expected result, `WF_RUN` drains, and the raw-state checker finds exactly 1,000 invocations, 1,000 terminal journals, and 4,000 entries with no gaps. Two normal local runs passed, the stronger with 33 handlers entered before kill; a race-instrumented run also passed with 32 entered. The old pinned worker's closed connection is expected when the fixture kills its server. The per-push chaos smoke job now includes this test. This covers a short-workflow full-restart slice, not the full Tier 2 matrix.

Tier 1 native timer scheduling now models a loss of schedule quorum across the due time, followed by a seeded 0–20-second virtual recovery delay. The integrated production-worker timer workload then verifies one terminal result and a resume within 30 virtual seconds of heal; seed 6 with a five-second delay is pinned for exact trace replay. A new real three-node contract isolates one node and stops another before a native schedule is due, then heals routes and observes the target with only two live nodes. Seven local two-survivor runs passed; target visibility ranged from 7.07 to 11.63 seconds after route heal, and the regular test also verifies the restarted third node reads the same target sequence. An earlier short-deadline version of the fixture timed out once before a node restart; its cause remains unconfirmed. The model does not claim NATS delivers immediately at heal. This is a focused timer contract, not the full route-fault matrix.

A further Tier 1 workload now runs the production worker with eight durable timer handles through the modeled schedule and durable consumer transports. One thousand seeded schedules cover simultaneous due wakeups, a schedule-quorum cut across the due time with 0–20 seconds of virtual recovery delay, a consumer-leader change, and a committed run acknowledgment whose reply is lost. All eight timer targets drain to one 35-entry terminal journal; the raw-state checker finds one immutable result. Exact replay for the first ten seeds, byte-identical seed-42 traces across two processes, and a focused race-instrumented run pass. This models the timer burst added to the real mixed workload without asserting server-side recovery timing.

An opt-in ten-invocation real-cluster mixed workload now seeds a 40/30/20/10 mix and the killed nonleader, pause timing, and delayed-store latency: four held short handlers, three native timers, two signal waits, and one six-child fan-out. It waits for the suspended workloads before replaying the same four server faults, holds quorum loss for 12 seconds, then requires all ten parents and six children to complete, the restarted node to serve their immutable results, delayed store syscalls to be recorded, and the final raw-state checker to find sixteen terminal invocations and journals. Seed 42 passed with the final suspension and one-consumption checks; seeds 1–3 and one race-instrumented run passed before those last audit assertions were added. The varied fault schedules for seeds 1 and 42 passed locally. The per-push chaos job now includes one seeded mixed batch, and a manual `tier2-mixed` workflow can run 20 or 200 consecutive seeds with replayable schedule artifacts and an optional starting seed for focused CI replay (default 1 for the gate); the fixed-timing and varied-timing 20-seed runs both passed before the new latency gate. The mixed test now records each parent's terminal journal server timestamp and gates p99 under 30 seconds from the later of recovered journal quorum and the last enabling event: effect release, timer due, committed signal, or final child completion. A result-polling estimate from quorum recovery alone reached 31.13 seconds on seed 1, while its last-event terminal p99 was 29.28 seconds. Seeds 1 and 42 passed this gate locally at p99 29.28 and 7.36 seconds; the first 20-seed run with this gate stopped during post-restart audit at seed 11, described below. A transient 503 during successor worker setup after quorum confirmation prompted bounded initialization retries. This is a small mixed slice; it does not yet satisfy the plan's ten-minute per-seed run, full 20-seed fault matrix, or 200 consecutive clean seeds.

The first latency-gated 20-seed mixed run passed seeds 1–10 and failed at seed 11 after all ten parent results were observed: the serial post-restart audit exhausted its four-minute test context before looking up `WF_SIG`. A local seed-11 replay reproduced that endpoint once, while three instrumented repeats passed with millisecond audit reads. The audit now checks the ten parents and six children concurrently and reports each read's elapsed time. The 20-seed latency gate still needs a clean rerun; the failed run did not establish a terminal p99 violation.

The next 20-seed mixed run passed seeds 1–11, including seed 11 with a 28.98-second terminal p99, then stopped at seed 12 after all ten parent results because the restarted node's first `WF_JRN` stream lookup consumed the four-minute test context. The failure did not report a terminal p99 violation. That lookup now retries with a three-second request deadline and a 30-second readiness budget, reports elapsed time and attempts, and saves all three server logs as CI artifacts on failure. A local seed-12 replay passed with an 18.06-second terminal p99; the 20-seed gate still needs a clean rerun.

The bounded-readiness 20-seed mixed run passed all 20 consecutive seeds at `80d573c`; a local seed-12 run showed the restarted `WF_JRN` lookup needed a second three-second attempt. Separate seed-12 repeats then found a genuine terminal p99 of 30.14 seconds for a short workflow, just beyond the 30-second gate. A live worker whose heartbeat cancels an in-flight run now releases its lease, publishes a deduplicated handoff run keyed by the original stream sequence, and naks the original delivery. This gives a recovery path when a nak sent without consumer quorum disappears. The Tier 1 heartbeat handoff workload now observes the extra run and proves one terminal result; local seed-12 repeats with the change passed at p99 29.30, 6.16, and 6.76 seconds, with five handoff enqueues from the first worker in each. One repeat still had heavy lease contention and little margin below 30 seconds, so the broader latency gate remains open for the changed worker. The 45-second worker-partition test also passed.

The bounded-readiness 20-seed run at `80d573c` passed, but its two slowest terminal p99 values were 29.98 and 29.99 seconds with the original 30-second default consumer `AckWait`. Because redelivery at that timeout leaves no processing margin under the 30-second gate, the worker default is now 20 seconds with a five-second progress heartbeat; explicitly configured 30-second control consumers are unchanged. Three local seed-12 repeats with the shorter default passed at terminal p99 24.64, 24.32, and 9.02 seconds. The consumer-leader kill test and full Tier 1 suite passed after the change. A new 20-seed and 200-seed mixed run on this revision remain required.

The Tier 1 heartbeat handoff model now includes a dropped nak request. The first worker still publishes its durable handoff and stops, while the original delivery retains its AckWait deadline. The successor completes from the handoff and later drains the original delivery without a second terminal result. Seed 11 pins the dropped-nak trace; the full simulator suite passed. This models one plausible client-visible failure mode behind the mixed-run latency without attributing the earlier behavior to NATS.

A three-node dispatch contract now compares that modeled dropped-nak state with a real durable consumer whose nak is withheld before send. The handoff arrives while the original remains pending, the original redelivers after AckWait, and both messages drain. Three normal repeats and one race run passed. This validates the transport state used by the Tier 1 trace; it does not establish that the earlier mixed-run latency was caused by a lost nak.

A second three-node dispatch contract compares the model and real JetStream after a successful one-second `NakWithDelay` with a four-second `AckWait`. Both redeliver the original once and drain it on ack. Three normal repeats and one race run passed. This covers the delayed-nak transport edge used by worker lease-contention retries.

The first 20-seed mixed run with the 20-second default `AckWait` passed seeds 1–10, then failed at seed 11 after every parent and child result passed the restarted-node audit. An unbounded `WF_SIG` stream lookup consumed the four-minute test context before signal timestamps and terminal p99 could be computed. That lookup now uses three-second requests within a 30-second readiness budget and reports elapsed time and attempt count. A local seed-11 replay passed with a 5.86-second terminal p99. The server-side cause of the original stalled lookup remains unconfirmed; the 20-seed latency gate needs another clean run.

The concurrently launched 200-seed run on the same prior revision passed seeds 1–12, then also exhausted its context in the unbounded restarted-node `WF_SIG` lookup at seed 13, after all sixteen restarted-node result audits. The latency timestamp now comes from the surviving replica with bounded requests; the restarted node still independently serves every parent and child result and journal audit. This isolates the latency calculation from that replica's stream lookup without treating its earlier stall as explained. A local seed-13 replay on the survivor-read change passed with a 23.94-second terminal p99. The 200-seed gate remains open.

The rerun with bounded restarted-node `WF_SIG` readiness at `24bcfe1` passed all 20 consecutive mixed seeds, including the earlier failure seeds 11 and 13. The slowest per-seed terminal p99 was 24.67 seconds (seed 7), below the 30-second gate. A 200-seed run on the survivor-read revision was launched; this 20-seed pass alone did not establish the full matrix or 200-seed release gate.

That [manual 200-seed mixed CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36552106923) passed all consecutive seeds 1–200 at `c1c6a83` in about two hours. Its slowest per-seed terminal p99 was 25.31 seconds at seed 193; four seeds were at least 25 seconds, and none reached 30 seconds. Every seed completed the ten-parent/six-child four-fault fixture and its retained-state and restarted-node audits. This clears the 200-seed count for that specific small mixed slice. It does not cover every chaos-matrix cell, the planned ten-minute workload per seed, or the Tier 3 soak.

The `tier2-mixed` workflow now runs 20 consecutive seeds on each push to `main` and is scheduled daily at 03:17 UTC for 200 consecutive seeds starting at seed 1. Both retain replayable fault-schedule artifacts, and manual runs still accept 20 or 200 seeds with an optional starting seed. These runs maintain coverage of the small mixed slice above; they do not expand that workload into the full Tier 2 matrix.

The mixed fixture's two signal-heavy invocations now each consume 16 ordered, uniquely keyed signals after route healing. The handler validates every payload, and the restarted-node audit verifies all 16 `SignalConsumed` entries per invocation have increasing stream sequences and matching payloads. Local seeds 1, 2, and 42 passed with terminal p99 values of 2.62, 16.34, and 14.56 seconds respectively. The earlier 200-seed result exercised the prior one-signal version; 200 consecutive seeds for the expanded signal workload remain open.

The [per-push 20-seed run at `d8345d6`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36652320167) passed all consecutive seeds 1–20 with 16 ordered signals per signal-heavy invocation. Its slowest terminal p99 was 16.05 seconds at seed 12. That revision still used one timer per timer-heavy invocation.

The same fixture's three timer-heavy invocations now each create eight durable native timer handles before the server faults and await all eight afterward. The pre-fault journal audit requires eight distinct timer names and server-recorded deadlines per invocation; the latency gate uses the latest deadline for each. Local seeds 1, 2, and 42 passed with all 24 timers scheduled, all results and terminal journals retained, and terminal p99 values of 14.61, 7.88, and 15.05 seconds. This still does not exercise the full Tier 2 fault matrix.

The [manual 200-seed run at `d6caa87`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36643687337) passed all consecutive seeds 1–200 with the earlier one-signal, one-timer workload. Its slowest terminal p99 was 26.91 seconds at seed 103; all 200 tests passed. The [first per-push 20-seed run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36651971159) also passed at `65399ac`, before the signal and timer workload expansions. Neither result proves the expanded fixture or the full matrix.

The [first eight-timer per-push run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36653046266) failed on seed 1 before route cuts: `strace` had not attached to the disk-fault node within the fixture's three-second readiness window. The saved server log showed that node running; tracer stderr was empty, so the cause is unconfirmed. The fixture now waits up to ten seconds for confirmed attachment and still fails without it. Two focused disk-fault fixture runs and a local mixed seed 1 passed after the change. The [next per-push run at `8da7bfc`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36653356756) passed all consecutive seeds 1–20 with eight timers and 16 ordered signals per mixed workload; its slowest terminal p99 was 14.49 seconds at seed 9.

The mixed fan-out slice now has two descendant levels. Each of six children durably starts two grandchildren and suspends before the server faults; after healing, twelve grandchild effects return 3 or 4, the children each return 7, and the parent returns 42. The restarted-node audit checks every result and terminal journal, and the raw-state checker requires 28 terminal invocations. The terminal p99 gate now includes all 28 invocations, using each child's last grandchild completion and each grandchild's effect release as their enabling events. Local seeds 1, 2, and 42 passed this expanded gate at 9.31, 17.90, and 18.79 seconds. A race-instrumented seed-1 run passed the 28-invocation gate at 6.97 seconds. The 20- and 200-seed gates for the deeper workload remain open.

The clarified route-fault timer gate passed a second full 10,000-invocation run: raw `fire_at` p99 36.60 seconds, post-heal p99 18.36 seconds, and post-heal maximum 22.89 seconds, with zero early or stuck completions and every result and journal audited. A 1,000-invocation repeat passed at post-heal p99 28.42 seconds. Another 1,000-invocation run failed during result auditing before its p99 calculation; the inspected invocation had already reached a completed journal and result. That smaller failure remains unconfirmed. See [route-fault timer results](scale/timer-route-faults-2026-09-28.md).

The timer result audit now waits up to 45 seconds for a terminal journal after `Await` returns a terminal result, reporting the last entry kind and read error if it remains absent. A subsequent 1,000-timer diagnostic completed all results and journals but missed the post-heal 30-second p99 gate at 30.98 seconds, with 22,521 redeliveries and 21,611 lease contentions. This uses 1–10-second sleeps and is more synchronized than the specified full 1–60-second workload; the cause of its recovery tail is still under investigation.

A third full 10,000-timer route run passed after the audit change: raw p99 31.23 seconds, post-heal p99 16.90 seconds, post-heal maximum 19.00 seconds, all results and terminal journals audited, and zero early or stuck completions. The clarified full-scale route gate has now passed three times; the shorter synchronized diagnostic remains a separate open latency case.

A fresh 1,000-timer, 1–10-second route diagnostic passed with post-heal p99 13.62 seconds, raw p99 35.00 seconds, and all results and journals audited. It recorded 2,483 redeliveries and 1,674 lease contentions. The earlier 30.98-second miss had much higher contention, so this passing rerun does not close the synchronized-tail investigation.

The current worker defaults also passed the opt-in 10,000-short-workflow dispatch proof across six workers and all 64 partitions. Starts took 2.44 seconds, the work queue drained in 14.63 seconds, exactly 10,000 handlers entered with no concurrent-handler marker collision, and the test checked every result plus the retained invocation and journal counts. This is a no-fault throughput and safety baseline, not a mixed-chaos proof.

A new opt-in live large-input test ran 1,000 unique JSON inputs just over 1 MiB through Object Store upload and six workers. It validated every full input, result, retained invocation and journal count, and the drained run queue. The full local run passed in 24.70 seconds, with starts in 20.61 seconds and all results in 20.93 seconds; the three replicas temporarily used about 3 GiB. The first full run reached all results in 1m40s but took ten minutes overall, so its later delay remains unlocalized. A focused control then showed that a partition loop could remain blocked on an open batch message channel after cancellation; the production loop now selects on its context while reading that channel. The worker and simulator suites, focused race test, and repeated live large-input run passed after that change. This is 1,000 live large inputs, not the 100,000-ID live-payload scale target. See [scale results](scale/README.md#live-large-inputs).

A further full large-input repeat checked the third replica's Object Store listing and found exactly 1,000 distinct `input-` objects. It again validated all results and retained counts, passed in 20.28 seconds, and shut down all workers in under one millisecond after cancellation. The original ten-minute completion remains unlocalized, but the repeat no longer shows a shutdown delay.

The first manual `large-input-scale` GitHub Actions run at `c7113ba` passed the same 1,000-object live proof in 14.65 seconds of Go test time. Starts took 9.22 seconds, all results were checked by 10.21 seconds, and all six workers stopped in 134 microseconds after cancellation.

The `6e5f868` per-push cluster job failed in the 30-day timer retention fixture before its first restart: the `Suspended` journal was present, but the original start run remained retained until the fixture's 45-second context expired. The fixture had stopped its worker immediately after seeing `Suspended`, which can precede the worker's acknowledgment of that run. It now waits for the run to drain while the worker is live, then stops the worker and performs both full-cluster restarts. Five repeated three-node runs and a focused race run passed. The fixture still checks that the timer schedule survives both restarts; it does not advance the server clock or prove the timer fires after 30 days.

The full-cluster-restart fan-out matrix row now has a Linux process fixture: it waits until six child invocations and the parent suspension are retained, stops the first worker, kills all three NATS processes, restarts them on their original stores and ports, and resumes the parent and children. It requires six distinct child IDs, result `7` for each child, parent result `42`, and seven terminal retained invocations and journals. An early repeated run found that account metadata could recover before the `WF_RUN` stream lookup; worker initialization now retries for up to 30 seconds after the restart. Five normal repeats and one race-instrumented run passed after that test fix. The `e8b62e7` per-push chaos job passed this row; its full cluster job remains in progress.

The Tier 1 run transport now treats an empty message ID as no deduplication key, matching a three-node `WF_RUN` contract: two publishes without `Nats-Msg-Id` retained two messages, while the same nonempty ID retained one within the window. A deterministic missing-ID negative control verifies that stripping the ID creates a duplicate run instead of letting the model hide it. This covers the transport edge of one planned chaos mutation; the full six-mutation chaos gate remains open.

The Tier 1 start model now checks I5 for retained invocations that have no journal: each must have a generation-matched `WF_RUN` message. The seeded 20-start workload verifies missing runs before repair and their presence after repair. A skipped-reconciler control makes the checker fail, and a reused-ID control shows why an old journal must be purged before its invocation: the old marker suppresses a new start repair, while the liveness checker still identifies the new generation's missing run. These controls are narrower than the full mixed-workload mutation gate.

A three-node journal mutation control now publishes `Started` and two competing index-1 entries without the expected-last-subject CAS header. Both the production journal reader and the raw-state invariant checker reject the retained duplicate-index history. A second three-node control appends a CAS-valid history with two worker IDs in the same epoch, representing a skipped lease; the raw-state checker rejects it. A third checks a completed invocation before deliberately purging `WF_INV` ahead of its journal; the raw-state checker detects the orphan journal. Together with the missing-message-ID transport control, these exercise detection paths for four of the six planned chaos mutations. The seeded replay workload already rejects changed step names and inputs, and the start-repair contract detects an invocation with no run message. These narrow controls do not yet constitute the full mixed-workload mutation run.

The worker's child-to-parent terminal notification now runs as a production decision through the modeled client signal transport. A 1,000-seed workload retries dropped or unacknowledged signal and wakeup publishes, retains one generation-bound parent signal and wakeup, and verifies that a reused parent ID fences an old child. The signal liveness checker also runs after seeded client signal calls and before and after the 20-signal client-to-worker drain. The earlier child-notification slice starts after a fixture terminal outcome. A new integrated worker workload now runs the parent and child handlers through lease, journal, result KV, terminal notification, and parent resume in one model. It covers uncertain child step, outcome, signal, and wakeup writes plus a consumer-leader change across 1,000 seeds, and checks one generation-bound notification and two terminal results. A three-node outcome contract compares model and real idempotence, immutability, and tombstone generation handling; three repeats passed. TCP proxy contracts hid committed KV create and tombstone-replacement update acknowledgments. Retries preserved the original payload and revision, matching the model; each contract passed three normal repeats and a race run. The model now has a separate post-update confirmation-read loss fault, representing the proxy cut after a committed update.

A second integrated Tier 1 child workload now runs production parent, child, and two grandchild handlers through the modeled durable consumer. A seeded scheduler chooses among pending run subjects after both descendant levels are durable, including notification wakeups that interleave with the second grandchild. One thousand schedules cover a dropped or unacknowledged grandchild step completion, lost notification signal or wakeup acknowledgments, and a consumer-leader change. All four invocations finish with immutable results, both leaf effects run only as permitted by their append outcome, the run queue drains, and the retained-state and signal-wakeup checkers pass. The first ten traces replay exactly, seed 42 is byte-identical across processes, and the focused race run passes. This is a Tier 1 reproduction path for the two-level real-cluster fan-out slice, not a model of server Raft or disk faults.

The journal model now supplies live-message reads to production `journal.Store.Read`, which verifies indices, epochs, and terminal order over retained model messages. The retained-invariant and workflow-replay workloads reload every completed journal through that path before checking the independent raw snapshot. A focused control accepts global stream-sequence holes and rejects a missing journal index after two seconds of virtual retries. The three-node contract compares real and modeled records and tails after interleaving two subjects; three repeats and a race run passed. Compacted snapshot reads now use a separate modeled manifest/Object Store port: 1,000 seeds advance the manifest twice, purge the covered live prefix, and recover the same logical journal despite one stale manifest or transient object read. Corrupt object bytes fail closed after bounded virtual retries. A three-node contract compares the model with real manifest bytes, object bytes, records, and tails after two compactions. Snapshot write and purge decisions now share a second modeled port: 1,000 seeds run production `MaybeSnapshot`, `SnapshotPrefix`, and `PurgeSnapshot` through object upload, manifest CAS, fixed-bound journal purge, and consumed-signal purge. Dropped requests and committed writes with lost acknowledgments retry to the same logical journal. The three-node contract now runs both real and modeled production snapshot writes and compares both compactions byte for byte. A 1,000-seed integrated worker workload now runs 130 production `wf.Run` steps, invokes the ordinary 256-entry snapshot cadence, and retains 16 live entries plus a verified snapshot. Object, manifest, and purge uncertainty retries without rerunning any effect; the reconstructed I1/I2/I3/I6 state passes. Two concurrent production snapshot writers now run through cooperatively scheduled modeled transport calls across 1,000 seeds. They request different retained suffix lengths and compete on the manifest revision CAS. A stale longer-prefix writer cannot purge entries absent from the winning shorter-prefix snapshot. Dropped requests and lost acknowledgments at object upload, manifest update, and bounded purge are repaired by a later compactor call. The manifest advances once or twice depending on the interleaving; the live suffix always matches it, and every logical record reconstructs. Pinned seeds 1 and 4 include a CAS conflict with a dropped purge or lost manifest acknowledgement; exact replay and cross-process seed 42 agree. A three-node contract now gates two real compactors after both read the same KV manifest revision. Across ten distinct journals per run, it checks one successful CAS, one `ErrSnapshotStale`, the winning manifest, complete logical reconstruction, and the exact retained physical suffix for different keep lengths. Five repeated runs and a race run passed.

A new modeled-worker constructor runs production `Worker.handle` over narrow invocation, signal, lease, journal, outcome, and dispatch ports. A 1,000-seed workload starts and completes five short `wf.Run` workflows per seed. Committed `WF_RUN` enqueues now feed the modeled durable consumer directly, including a lost reply; a dropped enqueue is repaired by production `StartScan`. It distinguishes a dropped step-completion publish, which reruns an effect, from a committed publish with a lost reply, which replays without rerunning it. Hidden terminal KV and run acknowledgments plus a consumer-leader change also drain to five unique terminal results. The raw retained-state checker passes I1/I2/I3/I6 after each seed, and the trace replays across processes and under the race detector. A new 1,000-seed integrated workload interrupts a running `wf.Run` effect through the production worker cancellation-notification handler. It covers a stale-generation notification, dropped and hidden cancel publishes, uncertain wakeup enqueues, and one journaled `SignalConsumed` plus `Failed` without a `StepCompleted`; the I1/I2/I3/I6 retained snapshot, exact replay, cross-process trace, and race run pass. The same production cancel-generation lookup now runs through a narrow port in both the real 15-second watcher and the simulator. The seeded workload withholds a core notification, advances virtual time to the poll, and verifies recovery; a stale retained generation is ignored before a matching one arrives. Two pinned traces cover a lost publish reply and the stale-then-matching poll. A three-node fixture unsubscribes and flushes the core notification before delivery, then verifies the real periodic poll interrupts the effect and retains exactly one canceled terminal journal. The real polling fixture passed three repeated runs and a race run. A 1,000-seed integrated worker workload now injects virtual heartbeat ticks while a `wf.Run` effect blocks. Production `Worker.handle` renews its modeled lease and calls `InProgress`; at the original AckWait boundary the modeled durable consumer redelivers without progress and stays quiet with an early, late, or repeated progress heartbeat. All paths finish with one effect, one terminal result, and an I1/I2/I3/I6 snapshot. Seed 42 is pinned and replays across processes and under the race detector. A three-node differential contract compares real and modeled progress deadline extension; three repeated runs and a race run passed. A second 1,000-seed workload hands one blocked `wf.Run` between two production workers after a modeled renewal request is dropped, a committed renewal reply is lost, a progress write fails, or the injected tick source closes. The first worker cancels its effect, naks the run message, cleans up its lease, and leaves only `StepRequested`; the successor redelivers, acquires a higher epoch, reruns the effect once, and writes the sole terminal result. Its I1/I2/I3/I6 retained check, exact replay, cross-process seed 42, and race run pass. Pinned traces include the lost-renewal reply and failed progress write. A three-node worker-level fixture now hides a committed lease-renewal reply during a blocked effect, then verifies cancellation, a retained `StepRequested`, successor replay under a higher epoch, one terminal result, and a drained run queue. Three repeated runs and a race run passed; the existing lease and heartbeat contracts independently check the component responses. Another three-node worker-level fixture injects a failed `InProgress` response at the dispatch boundary while the lease, journal, nak, redelivery, and successor execution use real JetStream. It checks the same unfinished-step handoff and drained queue. The same fixture closes an injected heartbeat tick source during the blocked effect and checks that handoff as well; both modes passed three repeated runs and a race run.

Another 1,000-seed workload now runs that worker across a suspension boundary in the model. Production `Client.Start` and `Client.Signal` feed the shared modeled run stream; `Worker.handle` journals `Suspended`, then drains a signal and completes on its next delivery. Lost signal publish replies and dropped or unacknowledged wakeup enqueues are reconciled by production `SignalScan`; completion append and run-ack faults, plus consumer leader changes, exercise replay and redelivery. The final raw snapshot passes I1/I2/I3/I6, signal liveness is clear, and the trace replays across processes.

A third 1,000-seed integrated worker workload runs a native timer from production `wf.Timer` through modeled scheduling, virtual-time target delivery, and resumed `Worker.handle` replay. The dispatch model now retains timer headers and the server timestamp used by `TimerHandle.Await`. Dropped and lost-ack timer publishes, completion appends, timer run acknowledgments, and a consumer-leader change all reach one terminal result. The due-time boundary, retained source count, I1/I2/I3/I6 snapshot, and cross-process trace replay pass. A further 1,000-seed workload now connects production fallback timer scheduling, `FallbackTimerScan.Scan`, and the resumed worker through one modeled durable consumer. Lost timer publish replies, scanner wakeup and delete uncertainty, completion append uncertainty, run acknowledgment loss, and consumer-leader movement all finish with one terminal result. It checks the due-time boundary, timer deletion, I1/I2/I3/I6 retained state, and exact replay across processes. A second 1,000-seed integrated workload now runs the production leased fallback poller twice around a cursor handoff, including dropped and hidden-ack wakeup, delete, and cursor writes, before the modeled worker resumes to one terminal result. Its dropped-delete trace is pinned and replays across processes. A result Object Store port now lets production `wf.Run` and `Worker.handle` spill and reload large step and terminal results in the model. One 1,000-seed workload covers dropped and acknowledged-but-unconfirmed object writes, lost journal and terminal KV acknowledgments, and consumer-leader movement. Step object write uncertainty now makes the worker retry instead of recording a permanent failure. A temporarily unavailable read of an already journaled step result also retries without altering that journal; its seed is pinned separately. It verifies exactly two retained content-addressed objects, hashes, result bytes, effect counts, terminal immutability, I1/I2/I3/I6, and cross-process replay. A fourth integrated worker workload now selects between a native timer and a signal across 1,000 seeds. It checks a signal before due time, a buffered signal when both are ready, timer-only completion, uncertain signal and timer publishes, and consumer-leader movement. The selected branch and result are retained once; a later timer delivery after the signal wins increments the cancelled-no-op metric without changing the journal or terminal KV. The I1/I2/I3/I6 snapshot, signal liveness, exact trace replay, and cross-process trace equality pass.

The production timer repair scanner now has a narrow transport port shared with the invocation, journal, and run-queue model. A 1,000-seed workload covers due and future timers, completed and terminal journals, invocation holes, dry runs, repeat scans, and uncertain wakeup enqueues; a three-node contract compares model and real outcomes and retained run counts, with three normal repeats passed. Its production adapter caches the `WF_INV` stream handle; the opt-in 200-missing-schedule recovery test passed after that change. Native route-partition timing and the worker handler's timer replay still need simulation.

The production suspended-wait scanner now uses a narrow modeled port for invocation and journal reads, subject-filtered signal reads, and wakeup enqueue. A 1,000-seed workload covers due/future timers, timer/signal select, stale and consumed signals, unrelated subjects, terminal journals, invocation holes, dry runs, uncertain enqueues, and virtual time advancement. A second 1,000-seed workload runs ten due timer waits and ten matching signal waits through the leased reconciler loop, injects wakeup and cursor uncertainty, then replaces the scanner; the cursor recovers and all 20 wakeups remain unique. A further 1,000-seed cooperative workload interleaves two live suspended scanners at lease, cursor, wait, invocation, journal, signal, and wakeup operations; forced lease turnover and an uncertain enqueue retain ten unique wakeups. A three-node contract compares the filtered read across a deleted signal sequence, scanner candidates, and deduplicated wakeups with the model.

The worker's timer publication now runs through a narrow native/fallback port. A 1,000-seed workload uses production message construction for 20 timers per seed, injects dropped and committed-but-unacknowledged publishes, checks duplicate retries, and delivers native targets after virtual time advances. A three-node contract compares retained native headers, fallback timer payloads, duplicate acknowledgments, hidden post-commit acknowledgments, and one routed target per native timer. This models the basic schedule contract; the real route-cut latency remains unexplained.

The fallback timer scanner now uses a narrow port shared with the timer publication model. A 1,000-seed pipeline scans 20 production-published fallback timers across due, future, purging, and tombstoned cases. It injects a lost wakeup acknowledgment and a lost timer-delete acknowledgment, then retries from the unchanged cursor and verifies one wakeup per eligible timer, deletion of retired timers, and later delivery of future timers. A separate 1,000-seed workload runs 20 due fallback timers through the leased production reconciler loop, injecting dropped or unacknowledged wakeup, delete, and cursor writes before scanner replacement. It checks persistent cursor recovery, 20 unique wakeups, and removal of every fallback timer. A further 1,000-seed workload interleaves two live fallback scanner loops at lease, cursor, cadence, timer read, publish, and delete calls. Forced lease turnover and uncertain wakeup and delete outcomes still leave ten unique wakeups and no timer records. The three-node timer contract compares the publish/delete cuts and retained outcomes against real JetStream.

The shared production reconciler loop now has a narrow port for lease acquisition and renewal, cursor load and CAS save, and cadence waits. A 1,000-seed workload runs production start or timer repair inside that loop, injects a dropped cursor write or a committed cursor write with a lost acknowledgment, then replaces the scanner. All 20 invocations retain one wakeup and the cursor survives replacement. Three-node tests verify saved-cursor takeover and stale revision rejection; another contract hides an acknowledgment after a real cursor create or update commits, then rereads and advances it from another node, with three race-instrumented repeats passed. A further 1,000-seed cooperative workload interleaves two live production start-scanner loops at lease, cursor, wait, and stream calls; a seeded cursor loss forces lease turnover, all ten wakeups remain unique, and five race-instrumented runs replay exactly. The native timer now reaches a modeled worker through the due target delivery; cooperative partition and scanner interleavings with that same timer remain outside this workload.
A new opt-in five-container NATS fixture builds the pinned server into a local scratch image, places each of five replicas on its own Docker file store and network namespace, and separates pinned client access from server route links. A corrected local run passed in 106 seconds: it checked that node four held 16 routes before disconnection, waited for its routes to fall to zero and the majority node to fall to 12, then completed one workflow on the four-node majority while node four could not observe the result during a two-second probe. Route healing, a container kill and same-store restart, immutable-result reads through the recovered node, and a retained-state audit then passed. An earlier repeat exposed that Docker network disconnection leaves existing route sockets alive for roughly 90 seconds; the fixture now waits for NATS route convergence. The [manual five-container CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36599468093) passed in 124 seconds with one invocation, one journal, two journal entries, and one terminal outcome. A subsequent three-run local repeat found a Docker lifecycle race: `docker kill` could return before an `--rm` container released its name, so a same-name restart failed. `KillNode` now waits for name removal; all three corrected repeats passed in 110.78, 113.76, and 111.03 seconds. The [follow-up clean CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36601536302) passed in 128 seconds at the fix commit. The fixture now races eight pinned majority-node `Start` calls after route convergence, requires one start and seven matching duplicates, and checks their client history with Porcupine. It also checks successful result reads across route healing and server restart against the immutable-result model. Two local live runs passed in 109.73 and 112.52 seconds. The second wrote an 11-operation JSONL history: one started, seven already-started, and three completed result reads. The [observed-history CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36602929845) passed in 121 seconds and its downloadable artifact has the same 11 operation outcomes. The worker now suspends on a signal during the partition: two same-key sends from different majority nodes return the same stream sequence, a changed-payload retry is rejected, Porcupine accepts the signal history, and the terminal journal contains one `SignalConsumed` entry. A local run passed in 109 seconds with 14 recorded operations. Three more fresh-cluster repeats passed in 112.68, 111.93, and 111.82 seconds. The [signal-history CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36604281917) passed in 125 seconds; its downloaded artifact contains all 14 expected operation outcomes. A second opt-in five-container test now SIGKILLs a five-replica file-stream leader during 1,000 concurrent publish attempts. It treats missing acknowledgments as unknown and audits every retained sequence and acknowledged payload through a survivor and the restarted leader. Local seeds 1–4 passed, with 956–964 acknowledged writes and 414–525 acknowledged after the kill. The [combined clean CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36606118005) passed both container tests: 960 raw writes acknowledged, 493 after node four was killed, and the signal workflow completed with the same 14-operation client-history artifact. The Docker fixture now explicitly configures the pinned server default `sync_interval=2m` and accepts `WF_TIER3_SYNC_INTERVAL` for the production value; local leader-kill audits passed at `2m`, `1s`, and `always`. The [clean `2m` CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36609558149) passed both container tests, acknowledging 964 writes, 511 after the leader kill. The [clean `always` CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36609575682) also passed both, acknowledging 964 writes, 536 after the kill. A leader-pause variant passed locally at `2m`: 956 writes were acknowledged, 455 after the current leader froze; the surviving majority retained every acknowledged write before the pause ended, and the resumed node served the same data. This is a process freeze, not a block-device delay. A separate route cut left two connected replicas and required that no publish acknowledgment occur without quorum; reconnecting a third replica restored acknowledgments, and both acknowledged writes were audited. Its local run passed in 99.68 seconds. The publish attempted during the cut has an unknown outcome. The [four-test `2m` CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36611043100) passed: 964 leader-kill writes with 489 after the fault, 956 leader-pause writes with 488 after the fault, and successful quorum-cut and workflow-isolation audits. The [four-test `always` CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36611047472) also passed: 952 leader-kill writes with 528 after the fault, 952 leader-pause writes with 518 after the fault, and both route-cut audits. The actual production interval, block-device stalls, clock skew, the full fault matrix, and the 24-hour soak remain unverified. See [five-container smoke](scale/tier3-container-smoke-2026-09-29.md).

`Client.Await` no longer uses its local wall clock to reinterpret a retained tombstone as `ErrNotFound` after its nominal expiry. The tombstone remains authoritative until the sweeper removes it, so clients with different clock offsets cannot disagree merely because cleanup is delayed. A three-node contract places an expired but unswept marker, reads `ErrPurged` from another node, deletes the marker, then reads `ErrNotFound`; three repeats passed. This addresses one SDK clock-dependence, not the full server/worker clock-skew matrix.

The five-container quorum-cut test now also records a `Client.Start` during the two-replica period and retries after a third rejoins. Its local run returned an unknown outcome with sequence zero during the cut and a successful start with sequence one after healing. Porcupine accepted the two-call write-once history, and the retained `WF_INV` stream held exactly one matching invocation. The manual container workflow uploads this history as a second JSONL artifact file.

The [clean `always` quorum-history run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36612428951) passed all four container tests. The [matching first `2m` run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36612424503) passed the leader kill, leader pause, and workflow isolation tests, but its quorum-history test received a transient JetStream 503 when reading back the invocation immediately after the retained stream reported one message. That final read now retries for up to 30 seconds while still requiring exactly one matching invocation; a full local rerun passed in 107.50 seconds. The [clean `2m` rerun](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36613756190) passed all four tests, and its uploaded quorum history records `unknown` followed by `started` with invocation sequence one. It acknowledged 960 writes in each leader-fault test, with 494 after the kill and 495 after the pause.

A [per-push CAS scale job](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36610592124) completed all 10,000 server-side races and reached the correct retained stream message count, then exhausted its shared ten-minute context during the serial 10,001-entry `journal.Read` audit. A separate three-minute audit context also expired locally: this read issues one API lookup per entry and took longer than that budget. The CAS proof now audits every retained entry through a batched ordered consumer, checking index continuity, stream sequence order, epoch monotonicity, alternating entry kinds, and writer identity; `journal.Read` remains covered in separate journal tests. The full 10,000-round local proof passed in 70.33 seconds with 20 leader restarts and the complete batched audit. The [clean per-push CAS job](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36613747853) passed at this revision.

The production `journal.Read` now switches from serial next-subject lookups to one filtered pull consumer after 64 live entries. It continues to validate every decoded record with the same index, sequence, epoch, and terminal rules; missing records still yield `ErrGap` and trigger the existing snapshot-race retry. A real three-node test interleaved 300 entries with 75 entries for another subject, read the target in 260 ms, then deleted one middle entry and verified a gap error. The full 10,000-race test now additionally calls production `journal.Read` on all 10,001 retained entries under the worker's 15-second read deadline; the first local run with batched reads passed in 346 ms and the complete test finished in 78.57 seconds. The first opt-in 100,000-entry boundary run exposed an SDK behavior: `OrderedConsumer.Fetch` resets the consumer on each batch, and the read received a no-responder error after about 30,000 entries. The reader now uses one ephemeral filtered pull consumer across all batches and requests its deletion when the read finishes. A full local boundary rerun appended 100,000 entries in 33.65 seconds, rejected entry 100,001, and reconstructed all 100,000 entries with `journal.Read` in 684 ms; the test passed in 37.75 seconds. The [first clean boundary CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36615897528) passed in 35.67 seconds, with a 597 ms full read. The [final clean run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36616087484) passed at the consumer-cleanup commit in 48.58 seconds, with a 684 ms full read. The per-push unit, CAS, and fan-out jobs also passed at that commit; the cluster and chaos jobs remain in progress.

The opt-in 5,000-entry repeated-snapshot test then observed a no-responder pull immediately after the filtered consumer was created in a no-fault three-node cluster; the server-side cause is unconfirmed. The reader now retries this transient at the same stream sequence and recreates the consumer after repeated failures, with five consecutive failures as the bound. Every delivered record still passes `verifyNext`, so the retry cannot silently skip an index. A focused test injects a no-responder reply before the next record and checks recovery plus temporary-consumer cleanup. Three consecutive full snapshot/control runs passed after the change, followed by a fourth run and the 100,000-entry boundary proof; the latter reconstructed its journal in 633 ms. The [clean boundary CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36617135535) passed at this revision with a 882 ms full read of 100,000 entries. The [clean snapshot CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36617146371) passed three consecutive 5,000-entry comparisons with 19 snapshots each, in 16.44, 16.15, and 13.91 seconds.

The synchronized 1,000-timer, 1–10-second route-fault diagnostic passed three more consecutive local repeats under the heal-based p99 gate, at 14.98, 11.62, and 12.25 seconds. All 3,000 timers completed without early or stuck outcomes, and their terminal journals were audited. The earlier 30.98-second p99 miss remains unexplained; see [timer route-fault audit](scale/timer-route-faults-2026-09-28.md).

Two recent per-push `cluster` jobs exhausted their shared 20-minute `go test ./integration` deadline: one reported a five-minute context deadline in the 500-child journal-leader-restart test, and another reported a ten-minute context deadline in the 10,000-round journal CAS test. The per-push workflow now runs the fan-out tests and the CAS test as separate jobs with their own deadlines; the remaining integration tests retain the original cluster job. The [first split CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36599606828) passed both separate scale jobs: all three 500-child fan-out variants and the 10,000-round CAS test with leader restarts. The remaining cluster and chaos jobs also passed, so all five active jobs in that split run completed successfully. The earlier shared-suite timeouts were sensitive to how the long tests shared a deadline; their isolated passes do not prove the runtime issue cannot recur.

A later local `go test ./...` at `aa4ddcf` likewise failed as a shared-suite run: the 500-child journal-leader-restart test exhausted its five-minute context after the seeded cut at child 381, and the package reached its default ten-minute timeout 37 seconds into the subsequent heartbeat test. With the same seed and cut, the fan-out test passed in isolation in 10.14 seconds; the heartbeat test passed separately in 38.37 seconds. This reproduces the shared-suite timing problem rather than proving its cause. The [matching split push CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36637113380) passed its unit, cluster, fan-out, CAS, and chaos jobs at `aa4ddcf`. The split jobs are the broad verification gate; the local all-in-one command is not green.

| Phase | Implemented and checked | Still required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0: harness | Three in-process JetStream nodes, pinned clients, node kill and restart on the same file stores, deterministic fault schedule files, retained-stream integrity checks. A 10,000-publish plain-stream test kills the stream leader at a seeded point during concurrent writes, then audits every retained sequence and acknowledged payload on a surviving node; a one-replica control passes before the kill and fails the same audit afterward. The leader-kill test passed seeds 1–5. A client-side TCP proxy cuts and heals one pinned connection or holds server responses after forwarding client writes; three-node tests verify isolation, majority progress, reconnect, and real network-level lost acknowledgments. A separate route relay isolates one server from both peers without stopping it; a direct test verifies route counts change from 2/2/2 to 1/1/0 and back. A recorded `PartitionNodes(0,1)` event now cuts only that direct pair, with route counts 1/1/2, and restores all routes after healing; the fixture test passed three repeated runs. A separate three-process fixture builds the pinned NATS server and replays recorded route-partition and SIGSTOP pause schedules. Its route relay changes the live route counts from 8/8/8 to 4/4/8 for one cut pair and back after healing. A three-replica stream then acknowledges a majority write while its leader is stopped, and the resumed node reads that retained write. The same process fixture now replays `KillNode` against a stream leader, acknowledges a majority write while it is down, restarts it on the same ports and file store, and reads the acknowledged write from the restarted node; three normal and two race-instrumented repeats passed. The route relay startup order was corrected after the race detector found a proxy-slice publication race; the partition-and-pause test passed three normal and three race-instrumented repeats after that fix. One recorded schedule now partitions the two nonleaders, stops the leader, and kills one nonleader; after healing routes and resuming the leader, the two-node majority acknowledges the next write, and the restarted third node reads it. Ten normal and three race-instrumented repeats passed. A Linux `strace` adapter now applies the fourth `SlowDisk` verb to existing JetStream store files by delaying filtered write and sync syscalls; a three-replica test checks that delayed syscalls occurred and all 11 messages remained. A recorded four-verb schedule delays one survivor’s store, partitions the two nonleaders, stops the leader, and kills the other survivor; after healing, a majority write is retained and the restarted node catches up. Local seeds 1–20 and three race-instrumented repeats of seed 17 passed. The per-push 20-seed process-fault smoke job now requires `strace` and uploads the replayable JSON schedule if a seed fails. This remains narrower than the ten-minute mixed-workload Tier 2 matrix. The first four-verb GitHub run at `37dc1d4` failed because the runner denied `ptrace` attachment before any delayed storage call; the disk tests are now opt-in outside the chaos job, which configures the runner’s Yama ptrace scope. The next run at `178f06f` passed seeds 1–19, then seed 20 failed during server startup because a route proxy bound a monitoring port selected for a later node. The route relay now excludes all selected server ports; the `a12565d` GitHub `chaos-smoke` job passed all 20 four-verb seeds, including seed 20, and its unit job passed. An opt-in integration test now holds a production `wf.Run` effect across the same four server faults and a 12-second quorum loss, restores a two-node majority, and checks the terminal result, one retained invocation and journal, delayed store syscalls, and the restarted node’s immutable result. Three normal runs and a race-instrumented run passed locally. The `4ec0718` GitHub chaos job passed all 20 four-verb stream seeds and this production workflow check (47.31 seconds); its unit job passed too. A sibling workflow test now suspends on a three-second native timer before the four faults, keeps quorum unavailable for 12 seconds past its due time, and requires terminal completion and the same retained-state and restarted-node checks after healing. It passed three normal repeats and a race run locally; the `b98d0e8` GitHub chaos job also passed the timer proof and its preceding 20 four-fault seeds. A third variant suspends on `AwaitSignal`, resumes after healing through a same-key retry of a transient 503, and requires exactly one retained `SignalConsumed` entry; three normal and one race-instrumented run passed locally, with CI pending. An earlier local signal run returned the result but exhausted a 120-second overall context before its audit; the test now records completion time and bounds each audit attempt. The cause of that slow run remains unconfirmed. These are focused workflows, not the mixed ten-minute Tier 2 generator. Opt-in client histories and Porcupine models check starts, signal queue order and idempotency, and result immutability across purge and ID reuse. Three-node tests cover 500 concurrent starts, 10,000 signals from 100 callers, and 100 concurrent result readers. | The full chaos and 24-hour soak matrix remains open. Tier3 permits five VMs or containers; a separate five-VM gate is not required. Cross-VM timing is optional deployment validation. The early Linux `strace` fault filters existing files only; later block-device fixtures cover newly created files and dm-delay, with qualification limits recorded in the current snapshot. |
| 1: start | Write-once invocation, input hash comparison, large input Object Store, idempotent provisioning, start reconciler. SDK-boundary and TCP-proxy lost-ack tests commit `WF_INV` but hide the response; they verify matching and mismatched retries, missing enqueue repair, and the observed start history. Bounded publish attempts and post-publish reads retry uncertain starts with the same input; injected tests cover transient reads, a committed hidden acknowledgment, and a publish that never reached the server. A three-node test kills the `WF_INV` leader after 100 of 500 callers enter publication, verifies one invocation and one run message with 499 `ErrAlreadyStarted` responses, and checks a Porcupine history; it passed ten runs before the history check and five more with that check. The regular three-node scale test starts 100,000 distinct IDs and verifies exactly 100,000 `WF_INV` messages, 100,000 `WF_INV` subjects, and 100,000 `WF_RUN` messages. Its first full run completed the start calls in 4.4 seconds and increased the test process's post-GC heap allocation by 134 MB; this is not server RSS or a per-subject memory estimate. A second regular test repeats the 100,000-start count proof while isolating node 2 at 200 ms intervals. It verifies route loss and recovery, at least one start begun on the isolated node, and exact `WF_INV` subject/message and `WF_RUN` message counts after healing. Three repeated full runs passed, each with 32 attempts begun during isolation; one run required 84 bounded retries. A separate-process three-node harness filled both `WF_INV` and `WF_JRN` with 10M subjects each, queried exact counts through each node, and measured 3,365–3,574 MiB RSS per node with 0.116–0.427 ms median stream-info calls at the 10M checkpoint; see `docs/scale/` for the 1M, 3M, and 5M checkpoints and the memory guard. | Ten-million-subject live spilled-input traffic, remaining larger-payload fault coverage, and final-source release gates. Cross-stream atomic batches remain unavailable; the reconciler is required. |

Production `SignalScan.Scan` now has a narrow modeled transport: 1,000 seeds of 20 committed signals cover missed wakeups, lost or dropped enqueue acknowledgments, consumed and terminal journals, stale generations, purged sequence holes, absent invocations, and post-window repeat scans. Exact replay and byte-identical cross-process traces pass. A three-node scanner contract compares dry-run repair, repeated deduplication, stale-generation skipping, and a deleted sequence hole; three repeats passed. Another 1,000 seeded schedules cooperatively interleave fixture signal publication with production scan transport calls, including publication between a missing read and stream-info lookup; scanning from the returned cursor eventually repairs each order, with exact replay across processes. A third 1,000-seed workload runs production client signal decisions through a narrow port shared with the scanner model: dropped and lost-ack publishes, uncertain wakeup enqueues, matching and mismatched retries, terminal admission, stale generations, consumed-signal verification after purge, and SignalWithStart. A three-node contract compares SignalWithStart, retry outcomes, RequireRunning, and retained stream counts; three repeats passed, and existing real lost-ack fixtures passed three repeats. Another 1,000-seed cooperative workload now interleaves production client and scanner transport calls, including a lost signal publish acknowledgment and lost or dropped wakeup enqueue; repeated scans retain exactly one wakeup in every schedule and trace replay passes across processes. The production worker signal drain now has a narrow modeled port for high-water, subject-filtered next-message, and blob reads. Another 1,000-seed workload runs 20 drain fixtures per seed across purged holes, unrelated messages, stale generations, blob references, lost signal acknowledgments, failed journal appends, corrupt hashes, and replay without a second append. A three-node contract compares filtered next-message behavior, deletion, generation skipping, ordered consumption, and replay; three repeats passed. A further 1,000-seed pipeline runs production client signal, scanner, and drain decisions together: uncertain publishes and enqueues are repaired, 20 ordered signals are journaled once, post-purge matching retries verify consumed hashes, changed retries fail, and replay plus a later scan add no wakeup. Exact disk replay and byte-identical cross-process traces pass. A separate short-handler workload now runs the production worker delivery path through modeled dispatch, lease, journal, and result transports. The production partition fetch/retry loop now runs through a narrow modeled consumer port: 1,000 seeds of 20 messages cover virtual AckWait, redelivery, progress calls, and injected consumer-leader errors; a three-node AckWait contract passed three repeats and a race run. A second three-node contract confirms an unacked delivery survives client replacement and that two clients sharing the durable fetch distinct later messages; three repeats and a race run passed. A direct late-ack contract found that JetStream accepts an older delivery’s ack after redelivery and then accepts the newer duplicate ack; the simulator was corrected, and three repeats plus a race run passed. Version 3 traces now record a 100,000-choice limit and report pending actions on bounded livelock or unfinished actors on a caller-context stall; version 2 replay remains supported. A replay divergence in two-worker dispatch exposed a race between a submitted transport turn and its operation context cancellation. The cooperative runner now resolves submitted turns through the scheduler; a focused cancellation probe and 20 repeated race-instrumented dispatch runs pass exact replay. A bounded decision minimizer now releases recorded choices, retains only reproductions of the same invariant failure, and verifies the resulting trace by exact replay; a synthetic ten-choice failure shrinks and replays. The minimizer now also tries removing cooperative actors, records disabled actors in the minimized trace, and verifies exact disk replay; a two-actor failure probe removes its irrelevant actor. The unit CI job now makes one bounded minimization attempt after a saved Tier 1 failure and uploads both the original and reduced trace. It requires exact reproduction of the original transcript and error before shrinking; unreproducible traces remain available for investigation. A second 1,000-seed workload cooperatively runs two production partition loops against the same durable, with yields at fetch and acknowledgment boundaries; all ten messages drain and the trace replays across processes. It exposed a clean-shutdown error when cancellation arrived during consumer creation; the loop now exits normally. The original dispatch-only workload still uses a callback; the separate integrated short-handler workload executes production worker lease and journal decisions. Real TCP-proxy tests drop committed lease create, renew, and release acknowledgments, verifying safe orphan reclaim and successor-safe cleanup; a short-TTL bucket confirms expiry fencing. Each passed three normal repeats and a race run. Repeated lost-create-ack runs twice observed a cross-node read of the successor pre-initialization revision just after its epoch update acknowledged. The contract now retries briefly at the age boundary and polls for the initialized value; ten combined contract repeats passed.
