The cause of the cross-node read lag is unconfirmed. | Complete remaining modeled transport edges and real differential gaps, final-source comprehensive Tier 1 validation, 200 clean seeds across the whole sustained matrix, five-node 24-hour full-matrix soak, and the six-mutation mixed chaos release gate. Focused seeded worker/signal/timer/retention and mutation proofs are recorded below. |

## Configuration deviations verified against NATS

- [JetStream atomic batches commit inside one stream](https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream/streams), so `WF_INV` and `WF_RUN` cannot be started in one batch; the same applies to `WF_SIG` and `WF_RUN`. The plan now states the production two-write and scanner-repair contract on every supported version. The start and signal scanners repair the gaps.
- An opt-in mixed-version process fixture boots one actual NATS 2.11.17 server with two module-pinned 2.15 servers. It now tests automatic fallback provisioned through either the old peer or a new peer. Each order starts and completes a timed workflow, repairs a second invocation's missing run message from another peer, checks the matching retry, then SIGKILLs the old server and restarts it on its original store with the current binary. It checks three current replicas, both earlier immutable results through the upgraded peer, a third timed workflow started there, and three terminal audit records. The [earlier clean mixed-version CI workflow](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36644874669) passed the pre-upgrade fixture. The [first clean full-upgrade workflow](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36645418077) failed when the repaired result could not be read after upgrade. Instrumented local repeats reproduced this in 2/5 explicit-fallback runs: both a surviving peer and the upgraded peer reported retained `WF_INV` sequence 3 while terminal `WF_STATE.inv_seq` was 2. The source of the extra accepted generation is unconfirmed. `client.Start` now publishes the invocation with `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence: 0` in addition to the configured per-subject limit. The Tier 1 transport has a one-shot subject-limit bypass fault: its production `Start` retry preserves the first generation under that fault, and a control publish without the header creates a second generation. The full-upgrade test now checks the retained sequence immediately after the retry and reports direct invocation/state probes on a later result failure. Five focused real-cluster repeats of the formerly failing explicit-fallback order passed with the CAS header on the actual publish; the full Tier 1 suite and targeted vet passed. Two full repeats of both provisioning orders passed (four full upgrades), as did focused concurrent-start and model-to-cluster contracts. The [clean rolling-upgrade workflow](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36647229348) passed at `c18b252`. Real three-node purge-and-reuse, old scheduled wakeup, late child signal, and model-to-cluster tombstone contracts also passed with the new CAS header. A separate three-node differential contract removes `WF_INV`'s per-subject cap: three repeats confirm production `Start` preserves the first sequence through its CAS header, while an unguarded control publish creates and retains a second generation. This isolates the CAS behavior from the configured subject limit and matches the Tier 1 bypass fault. A direct guarded duplicate on the normally limited stream returned JetStream error 10071 (`wrong last sequence`) before the subject-limit error; the model now follows that precedence, and its pinned retained-invariant trace was regenerated from seed 42. Cluster-wide native-timer admission and the full rolling-upgrade fault matrix remain open.
- A new opt-in five-container mixed-version fixture starts one actual NATS 2.11.17 container beside four module-pinned 2.15 containers, with separate network namespaces and persistent stores. It automatically provisions a five-replica fallback deployment through a new peer, completes a timed workflow started through the old node, repairs a second invocation's missing run message from a new node, verifies the old-node matching retry, SIGKILLs and upgrades the old container in place, reads both immutable results through it, and completes a third timed workflow after upgrade. The original final raw-state audit required three terminal invocations and journals; the signal extension requires four of each, and the fan-out extension requires 11 of each. Its first local attempt reached the upgrade but `EnsureAuto` exhausted the overall context while checking stores; logs showed temporary no-quorum warnings for `WF_PURGE` and `OBJ_WF_BLOB`. The replica catch-up gate now checks all 11 provisioned streams and buckets before revalidating the deployment. Four subsequent local runs passed in 20.60–34.29 seconds, followed by a race-instrumented pass. The precise cause of the first slow store recovery remains unconfirmed. The [first clean five-container rolling-upgrade workflow](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36649125230) passed both its three-process and five-container jobs at `c164aa9`. The container test now records client histories, checks `Start` and `Await` with Porcupine, and exports JSONL; a local run passed with three start and five result operations. The [clean history-enabled rolling-upgrade workflow](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36649285949) passed both jobs at `bb2842a`; its downloaded JSONL artifact contains three start operations and five result reads. The fixture now also starts a two-signal workflow through the old node, waits for its durable suspension, upgrades the node, sends two ordered signals through different new-version peers, and checks the result and Signal history. Three local five-container runs and one race-instrumented run passed with the signal extension. The [clean signal-enabled rolling-upgrade workflow](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36649843481) passed both jobs at `3fe000a`; its downloaded history artifact contains four starts, six result reads, and two signals. The fixture now also starts a six-child fan-out through the old node, verifies six distinct durable child requests and parent suspension, upgrades the node, and runs successor child workers on the required partitions. The parent returns 42, every child returns 7, and the final 11-invocation raw-state audit passes. Three local runs and one race-instrumented run passed; a recorded history contains five starts, 13 result reads, and two signals, all checked by the existing Porcupine models. The [clean fan-out rolling-upgrade workflow](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36650416626) passed both jobs at `d669511`; its downloaded history artifact contains the expected five starts, 13 result reads, and two signals. The broader rolling-upgrade fault matrix remains open.
- Scheduled messages and their targets must be in one stream. The server rejects schedules with `DiscardNew`, so `WF_RUN` uses `DiscardOld` with unlimited messages, bytes, and age. Provisioning rejects limits that could silently evict live work.
- Per-message TTL deletes an unread message at expiry. The fallback keeps a `WF_TIMER` record without TTL and deletes it only after a due `WF_RUN` publish is acknowledged; TTL expiry cannot safely serve as the poller trigger. The fallback passed with scheduling disabled on the current three-node fixture and with an opt-in NATS 2.11.17 server binary.
- `EnsureAuto` now uses fallback scheduling for every fresh deployment, even through a new-version peer, and rejects an existing native `WF_RUN` stream. The connected peer version cannot prove cluster-wide scheduling support. Explicit native admission still checks the connected server is 2.12+ and requires operators to verify every peer. A three-node current-version fixture now proves fresh `EnsureAuto` selects fallback and rejects an already native `WF_RUN`; the worker runner uses explicit native mode for its pre-provisioned native fixture. Two repeats of both mixed-version process provisioning orders, two five-container mixed-version upgrades, and a five-container race run passed after automatic provisioning moved to the new peer. Automatic native admission remains disabled until cluster-wide version evidence can be supplied. The [clean fail-closed rolling-upgrade workflow](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36651320643) passed both jobs at `cfade8a`; its downloaded five-container history still has five starts, 13 result reads, and two signals. A focused NATS 2.11 contract twice confirmed explicit native admission rejects that peer before automatic fallback provisioning succeeds.
- The `wf-worker` command now accepts `-timer-backend fallback|native|auto`. An explicit fallback choice provisions a new cluster through a current server without relying on its local version as a proxy for every peer; a focused live runner test creates fallback `WF_RUN`, completes a timer, and drains `WF_TIMER`. The default `auto` now chooses fallback on a fresh mixed-version rollout; an existing native deployment must be restarted with an explicit `native` choice after all peer versions are verified.
- Retention purges `WF_TIMER` subjects for the retiring invocation sequence after its journal and before its tombstone. A crash injected after that stage resumes correctly, and records for other generations remain untouched.
- The fallback poller also removes records proven retired by a matching purge marker or tombstone. Workers renew their lease before timer publication; an extreme pause between renewal and publication can still leave a late record, which the poller removes while the retirement marker remains available.
- Lease creation revisions serve as epochs. They remain unique even when a lease expires before its first journal append.
- Scheduled timer publish IDs include the invocation sequence as well as the logical step, so a reused ID cannot deduplicate a new generation's schedule against an old one.
- Journal snapshots use a separate `snap.<type>.<id>` manifest in `WF_STATE` and a hashed object in `WF_BLOB`. Reads reconstruct the logical journal from the object and newer live entries. Compaction currently retains the newest 16 entries and purges with a fixed stream sequence bound, so later appends survive. The full-prefix object is rewritten at each snapshot; this is correct but costly for long journals.
- The long compaction test exposed brief read-after-write lag across replicas: an acknowledged snapshot object or KV manifest was sometimes invisible from a pinned node immediately afterward. Snapshot upload verification and bounded manifest/object read retries now precede purge. Persistent absence or hash mismatch still fails closed with `ErrGap`.
- Retention tombstones carry an expiry time that `client.Await` honors. `retention.SweepTombstones` removes expired KV entries once the old invocation is gone, with a revision precondition that protects concurrent replacement. The CLI exposes a one-shot sweep; deployments must schedule it. `retention.SweepBlobsQuiescent` can reclaim unreferenced Object Store data after clients and workers stop; online reclamation needs a coordination protocol because Object Store deletion does not compare metadata revisions.
- Projection rebuild uses retained `WF_INV` records and `journal.Read` (including snapshot objects), because compaction removes the original `WF_JRN` prefix. Its consumer lag counts unacknowledged journal messages; it does not include invocation-only starts or purges, which the periodic rebuild detects.

Most tests in `integration/` are correctness tests. The distinct-start tests establish the 100,000-subject count bar with and without route cuts, but the suite does not establish the larger memory, throughput, or fault-tolerance proof bars in the plan.

A full suite run after the Goexit/cancellation change exposed one transient `nats.ErrNoResponders` on the blob-sweep test's first Object Store upload. That test now retries only this startup response with a bounded delay; ten isolated and five paired reruns before the retry passed, five paired post-fix runs passed, and the next full `go test ./... -count=1 -timeout=25m` run passed (integration: 500.7 seconds). The server-side reason for the single response is unconfirmed. After search-attribute changes, a default-timeout `go test ./...` run hit the same first-upload response once and then timed out at ten minutes while running the full-cluster restart test. Those two tests passed together in isolation, and a clean full `go test ./integration -count=1 -timeout=20m` run passed in 675.2 seconds. The first-upload retry was absent from the current blob-sweep test file and has been restored; full-suite commands now document a 25-minute timeout.

After the live-cancellation change, one `go test ./... -count=1 -timeout=25m` run timed out in `TestSuspendedScanRepairsMatchingSignalOnly` at its 20-second context deadline. Ten isolated reruns passed, and a fresh full `go test ./integration -count=1 -timeout=25m` run passed in 685.4 seconds. The timeout cause is unconfirmed; that test now prints journal, run-stream, and loop/worker state if it recurs.

One earlier full-suite run reported 26 unexpected outcomes among the 500 no-fault concurrent starts. The assertion now reports unexpected errors if this recurs. Bounded publish and read retries address plausible transient causes; the original failure remains unconfirmed because its errors were not captured.

## Sustained leader rows and history-window correction

The signal history model now applies its two-minute duplicate-window bound to each identity (type, ID, invocation generation, name, and idempotency key). Distinct identities may span the sustained run while same-key expired retries remain refused. Global known-signal sequence and order checks remain in place. The saved ten-minute run's 1,872 operations passed the Start, Signal, and Await models after this correction. A 1,000-seed Tier 1 checker workload covers long histories with distinct keys, invocations, names, and generations, reversed order, and an expired same-key retry; it fails against the former checker, replays exactly, and pins seed 42. The full simulator and history suites and focused race runs passed. The prior commit `35a6a4d` also passed its clean full test workflow and 20-seed mixed-fault workflow. This is a checker regression, without a new broker transport assumption.

The sustained consumer-leader row shares the journal row's workload and audits. It prefers a durable with live deliveries, kills the node named by that consumer's own leader metadata, and records the consumer name and its pending and ack-pending counts. The normal 35-second smoke run passed 224 terminal invocations with a 7.01-second aggregate terminal p99; its selected durable had seven ack-pending deliveries at the kill. A race smoke run passed 196 terminal invocations with a 20.55-second aggregate terminal p99 and one ack-pending delivery at the kill. These are shortened runs, not ten-minute matrix evidence. The manual workflow now selects `journal` or `consumer` while retaining its existing YAML filename.

Both rows now retain a JSON liveness artifact even if a later checker fails. It records enabling and observed journal timestamps for each invocation's start, timer deadlines, committed signals, child completions, and terminal entry. Per-workload next-entry p99 is gated alongside terminal p99; maximum delays and counts over 30 seconds are reported, and early timer completion or signal consumption is rejected. A fresh 35-second consumer-leader run passed all expanded gates: eight batches, 224 terminal invocations, aggregate terminal p99 2.18 seconds, per-type next-entry p99 below 728 ms, maximum next-entry delay 7.22 seconds, and no enabling-event delays over 30 seconds. This remains shortened evidence.

The [100,000-seed Tier 1 run at `749c4eb`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36675754069) passed in 37m20.2s: 5,500,604 generated schedules, 157,551,853 scheduler choices, and 1,295,266,962 transport events. It covers the 32-contender expiry and stalled-cursor workloads, but predates the new signal-history-window checker workload.

## Sustained all-server SIGKILL row

`TestMixedMatrixAllServersKilledEveryThirtySeconds` adds the matrix row that kills all three server processes before restarting any of them. Restart uses the same file stores and ports. Heal requires leaders and two current, online replicas for each of the ten provisioned workflow streams, KV buckets, and Object Store streams. The shared workload, history, retained-state, enabling-event and terminal latency checks remain in force; this process-kill row uses raw enabling-event delay, without the route-quorum recovery adjustment. The manual matrix workflow selects this row with `cluster`.

The first shortened attempt had an incorrect recovery-gate name (`KV_WF_PURGE` instead of `WF_PURGE`) and failed at the bounded heal check. After correction, a 35-second normal run passed eight batches, 224 terminal invocations, and 2,476 journal entries. All three nodes were killed at +30.00 seconds and confirmed healed at +38.60 seconds. Aggregate terminal p99 was 3.25 seconds; every per-type terminal p99 remained under 30 seconds (the slowest was signal at 14.35 seconds). Timer next-entry p99 was 12.45 seconds, maximum enabling-event delay was 13.22 seconds, and no enabling-event delays exceeded 30 seconds. This shortened run does not establish the ten-minute row or the targeted mid-fan-out restart row.

The same seed also passed a shortened race-instrumented run: seven batches, 196 terminal invocations, 2,162 journal entries, and all three servers healed 6.56 seconds after the kill. Aggregate terminal p99 was 12.45 seconds, the slowest per-type terminal p99 was signal at 15.77 seconds, timer next-entry p99 was 7.07 seconds, maximum enabling-event delay was 12.45 seconds, and no enabling-event delays exceeded 30 seconds. Both runs passed all three history models and drained `WF_RUN`. Integration vet and workflow YAML parsing passed.

## Sustained majority-side server partition row

`TestMixedMatrixServerPartitionEveryThirtySeconds` isolates node 2 for ten seconds at each thirty-second boundary. The shared client and worker connection is restricted to nodes 0 and 1 and ignores discovered servers for this row, so workflow traffic stays on the majority side. Each fault confirms 4/4/0 server route counts and commits a replicated probe while node 2 is isolated. Heal confirms 8/8/8 routes, reads the same probe sequence and payload through node 2, and verifies all ten workflow stores have current, online replicas. Route counts, probe sequence, cut and heal times are retained in the fault artifact. The raw enabling-event p99 gate stays under 30 seconds because this majority never loses quorum. The workflow selector is `partition`.

An initial 45-second normal smoke passed eight batches, 224 terminal invocations, 2,474 journal entries, all three histories, and a drained queue. Its recorded partition routes were 4/4/0 and its majority probe sequence was 1. Routes healed 10.63 seconds after the cut. Aggregate terminal p99 was 3.48 seconds; the slowest per-type terminal p99 was signal at 17.77 seconds. Timer next-entry p99 was 6.77 seconds, maximum enabling-event delay was 17.61 seconds, and no delays exceeded 30 seconds. That run predates the additional post-heal probe read and workflow replica gate; fresh validation includes those gates. This is shortened evidence, not a completed ten-minute row.

Fresh partition race attempts exposed two named transient transport responses: `ErrNoStreamResponse` while publishing through an electing stream and API error 10008 (`JetStream system temporarily unavailable`) when reading the healed minority. Those responses now retry within the existing bounded controller context, preserving the probe's message ID. A subsequent attempt passed the majority probe but timed out waiting for `KV_WF_LEASE` replica catch-up. The controller now reports the last stream and full replica metadata on failure, and reserves 25 seconds after the deliberate ten-second isolation for replica catch-up. This changes the fixture's catch-up allowance; the raw workflow p99 gate remains under 30 seconds. A subsequent race run passed the stricter row: seven batches, 196 terminal invocations, 2,163 journal entries, all histories and a drained queue. The majority probe committed while routes were 4/4/0; the minority read and all-store replica checks confirmed heal at +61.18 seconds (21.18 seconds after route restoration). Aggregate terminal p99 was 2.92 seconds; the slowest per-type terminal p99 was fan-out at 13.29 seconds. Every enabling-event delay remained under 30 seconds. This is still a shortened run.

The [ten-minute journal-leader row](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36684091070) completed 50 batches, 19 leader kills, and a valid retained audit of 1,400 terminal invocations and 15,456 journal entries. The [ten-minute consumer-leader row](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36684093136) reached batch 60 and all 19 consumer leader kills, then failed its bounded retained-state checkpoint audit. The [ten-minute all-server SIGKILL run at `9ec6967`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36684634972) passed seed 1: 62 batches, 19 full-cluster kills, 1,736 terminal invocations and 19,153 journal entries. The cancellation replay's matching notification was recorded after it canceled the effect context. This allowed the worker actor's resulting writes to appear ahead of the notification in the transport trace depending on host scheduling. The test now records that delivery before invoking the production cancellation observer. The existing pinned trace remains unchanged. Ten race-instrumented repetitions of the 1,000-seed cancellation workload, its cross-process replay check and pinned regression passed after the ordering correction; a separate 100-repeat pinned replay also passed. This repairs the test scheduler's event ordering, without changing production cancellation behavior. A fresh extended run is required for this correction.

## Retained-state audit read recovery

The [first full-duration partition run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36686054221) failed its batch-10 checkpoint on API error 10008 during a journal reread. The integrity checker previously scanned every raw journal entry, then created independent filtered reads of every logical journal. It now checks the already scanned ordered records directly for journals without snapshots, including monotonic retained stream sequence validation. Journals with snapshot manifests still use production reconstruction and Object Store validation. Individual metadata, raw-message and terminal-KV reads have two-second attempts and three bounded retries for named transport timeouts/no-response and API 10008; semantic and invariant errors fail immediately. A lost reply retries its current sequence, preserving previously visited records.

Unit tests confirm current-sequence retry without duplicate visits, retained holes, bounded retry counts, cancellation and immediate semantic-error propagation. The integrity race suite and full simulator suite passed. Real three-node tests still reject two workers using the same epoch, reconstruct a purged snapshot, and reject its missing Object Store prefix. A shortened consumer-leader row passed with 196 terminal invocations, 2,159 journal entries, aggregate terminal p99 21.00 seconds, all history and per-type liveness gates, and a drained queue. This is local verification of the audit change; the full-duration consumer and partition audit gates remain open.

## Bounded serial journal reads

Serial `journal.Read` requests previously inherited the worker's fifteen-second read context. They now use two-second request contexts, retry a named timeout/no-response or API 10008 at the same next-subject sequence at most three times, and preserve all verified prefix records. A missing entry remains a semantic absence; the existing index, epoch, terminal and gap checks still apply. Exhausted transient retries report subject, sequence and attempt count while preserving the underlying error. Snapshot metadata reads and the batch-reader transport retain their existing paths; this is a candidate contributor fix, not proof that the earlier 42.47-second fan-out latency is resolved.

A new Tier 1 workload injects deadline, no-responder and API 10008 replies after a verified prefix. It checks one/two retries, named exhaustion, rejection of a deleted middle entry, exact records and tail, bounded virtual delay, exact replay and cross-process trace identity. Seed 42 is pinned. The workload fails against the former implementation and passed 100,000 local seeds in 11.71 seconds. The full journal and simulator suites and focused race/pinned-corpus checks passed. A real three-node TCP-proxy contract holds actual server responses until a second serial request begins, then releases them and verifies the unchanged full journal and tail. Its race run passed. That contract first found a mistake in the real retry-delay branch, which retained the previous error after waiting; the branch was corrected before the passing run.

The [partition row with the audit improvement](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36686731740) passed its formerly failing early checkpoint, reached batch 26 and seven partitions, then failed on a generic API 10008 from a client call. The existing thirty-second same-identity client retry now also recognizes that named transient error through the row's transport classifier. The preceding `5282e7a` full test workflow and 20-seed mixed-fault workflow both passed; the newer extended and matrix runs remain separate evidence.

The [full consumer-leader run with the audit change at `f775977`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36686729890) completed 74 batches and 19 faults and passed its retained audit of 2,072 terminal invocations and 22,874 journal entries. Its histories passed and aggregate terminal p99 was 5.03 seconds. The earlier checkpoint deadline did not recur, but fan-out terminal p99 still failed at 33.16 seconds. This run predates bounded serial reads; it verifies audit progress, not closure of the consumer latency gate.

## Snapshot manifest request recovery and partition probe timing

Snapshot manifest lookup now uses the same two-second, three-attempt read recovery as serial journal requests. Named timeout/no-response and API 10008 replies retry the manifest key; `ErrKeyNotFound` remains an immediate absence, and malformed manifests still fail with `ErrGap`. Object downloads and snapshot integrity checks retain their existing paths. A new seeded manifest workload covers all three transient response classes, one/two retries, exact exhaustion errors, a missing live entry after manifest lookup, virtual delay bounds, exact replay and cross-process identity. Seed 42 is pinned. The workload failed against the former manifest reader and passed 100,000 local seeds in 15.18 seconds. The full simulator suite passed in 44.14 seconds, and focused journal and simulator race suites passed. A real three-node TCP-proxy contract separately holds the manifest response until a retry begins, releases it and checks the unchanged logical journal and tail. Both the serial and manifest network contracts and compacted-snapshot recovery/corruption test passed under the race detector.

The [first partition run with bounded serial reads](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36687939027) failed before its first heal because the dedicated majority probe did not receive an acknowledgment within its separate six-second allowance. The probe now uses one-second attempts within the remainder of the deliberate ten-second isolation, retaining its message ID and retrying the named in-progress-duplicate response 10158. It still must receive a replicated acknowledgment before any route heals. Workflow raw enabling-event p99 remains under 30 seconds; the isolation and replica recovery checks remain required. The earlier six-second probe deadline was a fixture-specific limit, not a plan-defined workflow latency gate.

A shortened race run with the manifest retry and revised probe timing passed eight batches, 224 terminal invocations, 2,476 journal entries, all histories, all per-type latency gates and a drained queue. It confirmed 4/4/0 isolation and probe sequence 1, then full heal at +46.54 seconds. Aggregate terminal p99 was 9.98 seconds; timer and fan-out per-type terminal p99 were 20.25 and 18.75 seconds. This remains shortened evidence. Full journal and consumer gates from the prior commit remain independently pending.

## Sustained random worker process kills

`TestMixedMatrixRandomWorkerKilledEveryFiveSeconds` uses three actual worker subprocesses on the three-node cluster, each running production partition loops and the mixed handler set. Every five seconds it selects a worker with the seeded fault RNG, SIGKILLs it, verifies the OS exit signal, and launches a new worker generation. The artifact records PID, worker slot and identity, active-lease count at the kill, readiness/heal time, and per-generation logs and dispatch JSONL. Cleanup reaps children, and retained child race-detector warnings fail the parent test. Reconciliation stays in the parent process. Select `worker` in the manual matrix workflow.

The first normal smoke passed 224 terminals and six kills; a race smoke passed 112 terminals, but the normal run's selected workers were all idle at their kill points. That is harness evidence only. The row now gives short effects a two-second execution interval and requires at least one active-lease kill. The stronger race run hit two active workers among six kills, completed 84 terminal invocations and passed its retained audit and histories, then failed aggregate terminal p99 at 42.03 seconds. Two short invocations took 42.03 seconds and another took 22.02 seconds. The saved trace for one slow invocation shows its first lease acquisition, a second acquisition exactly twenty seconds later, then a third exactly twenty seconds after that; the first two owners were killed and the final effect completed in two seconds. Those gaps match the configured `AckWait=20s`, giving a concrete repeated-kill liveness case. The under-30-second gate remains in force; this row is not green, and its terminal failure precedes queue-drain verification. The existing Tier 1 retained-lease slices do not yet reproduce this successive-process-kill/consumer-redelivery sequence.

The [full partition run at `2d1151d`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36689217944) reached batch 40 and eleven confirmed partitions, then failed its retained audit on API 10008 while opening a store. The checker retries individual named transport reads; its outer three whole-audit attempts now recognize the same named transient responses after request retries are exhausted. Full-duration validation of that fixture recovery change remains open.

## Successive worker-kill delivery reproduction

A Tier 1 replay now combines the virtual durable pull consumer with production lease acquisition and journal append/read decisions for two repeated-kill sequences. The first owner dies before its first heartbeat. If the next targeted owner is killed at twenty-one seconds, `AckWait=20s` completes at 41.8–42.2 seconds while an experimental ten-second AckWait encounters the still-live twelve-second lease, NAKs for five seconds, then completes at 16.8–17.2 seconds. If instead the next targeted owner is killed at sixteen seconds, twenty-second AckWait completes at 21.8–22.2 seconds, while ten-second AckWait incurs a second delivery/lease wait and completes at 31.8–32.2 seconds. Both configurations require an unchanged four-entry terminal journal, rejected stale-owner renewals/appends, and a drained modeled consumer. This isolates delivery and lease timing; it does not run the full worker handler/heartbeat goroutines or model OS processes, and does not establish a universal bound under repeated kills.

Seed 42 is pinned. Exact replay, byte-identical cross-process trace checks, and the race-instrumented 1,000-seed/pinned regression checks passed. The expanded two-schedule workload passed 100,000 local seeds in 14.80 seconds across all six schedule/effect-duration combinations. The full simulator suite passed in 49.00 seconds, and integration/simulator vet passed. Runtime defaults remain unchanged. `WF_MATRIX_WORKER_ACK_WAIT` is an explicit experimental override for child workers in the real process-kill row; it records the selected timing in each child log.

A 35-second race-instrumented real-cluster run with ten-second AckWait killed six workers, including two active owners, completed 56 terminal invocations and passed retained-state and client-history checks, but failed terminal p99 at 32.03 seconds. One short invocation's trace shows acquisition at zero, a held lease on redelivery at ten seconds, acquisition at fifteen seconds followed by the second kill, another held lease at twenty-five seconds, acquisition at thirty seconds and completion two seconds later. This motivated the sixteen-second-kill model case. The latency failure precedes final per-type and queue-drain gates; the candidate is not a green matrix row and the production default is not changed.

## Lease-aligned default consumer redelivery

The default AckWait is now `provision.LeaseTTL + 1s` (thirteen seconds), retaining the three-second heartbeat and twelve-second lease TTL. This avoids a normal first redelivery before lease expiry while reserving enough time for a second killed owner and the two-second effect in the reproduced sequence. The expanded version-2 Tier 1 workload keeps both earlier configurations as controls and adds a fourteen-second kill that strikes the thirteen-second replacement before completion. All nine kill-time/effect-duration combinations complete at 14.8–15.2 seconds or 27.8–28.2 seconds with the new default, with immutable terminal journals, stale-owner rejection, and drained consumers. It passed 100,000 local seeds in 34.67 seconds, exact/cross-process replay and focused race/pinned checks. The earlier pinned workload remains replayable. Restoring the former twenty-second default makes the new test fail seed 1 at 41.8 seconds; the default was restored after that negative control. Worker, provision and simulator suites passed, with the simulator taking 65.54 seconds under concurrent verification. These modeled cases do not establish a bound for arbitrary numbers of kills or long effects.

A 35-second race-instrumented real process-kill run with the explicit thirteen-second candidate passed six kills (two active), 112 terminal invocations, all history/integrity/per-type latency gates and queue drain, with aggregate terminal p99 15.05 seconds. A second race run using the actual new default passed six kills (one active), 140 terminal invocations and 1,545 journal entries, the same gates and queue drain, with aggregate terminal p99 15.04 seconds. Both are shortened local evidence; the sustained worker row and consecutive-seed release gate remain open.

Existing durable consumers require an explicit coordinated timing update while their workers are stopped; `CreateConsumer` rejects a mismatch instead of adopting it. A real three-node upgrade contract checks that rejection, explicitly updates the consumer, verifies its pending delivery, delivery/ack-floor sequence and retained run payload are unchanged, then acknowledges the original delivery and checks the queue drains. The contract passed under the race detector. This migration preserves the durable rather than deleting and recreating it. The README documents the update and an explicit twenty-second compatibility configuration.

## Child completion wakeup checker and local matrix timeout

A retained-state Tier 1 checker now begins at terminal child journals and their invocation parent headers, so a skipped notifier is detected even when there is no signal for the earlier signal-only checker to inspect. It requires a current generation's matching consumed outcome, a matching notification with its retained parent wakeup, or a generation-matched terminal parent; obsolete parents and child generations receive named waiting reasons. Inline payloads must match even if hash metadata claims otherwise. Blob-backed notifications compare hash metadata; blob content verification stays in the production drain/object checks. The seeded child-notification workload checks missing obligations before publication, after injected losses, and after retries. Existing replay transcripts remain unchanged.

Fifteen focused cases cover skipped/dropped notifications, dropped or removed wakeups, altered notification and consumption payloads, consumed signals after purge, and parent/child terminal and generation cases. The focused race suite and existing pinned child traces passed in 19.82 seconds; 100,000 child-notification seeds passed in 146.89 seconds. The full simulator suite passed in 76.53 seconds and simulator vet passed. This adds child-completion I5 negative controls, not a full process-kill/scanner/worker pipeline.

The first local ten-minute worker-kill attempt at `1233488` omitted Go's explicit test timeout and was terminated by the default ten-minute timeout after batch 50. It produced no final audit or latency/queue result and is not a product latency failure or a clean row. Process inspection after termination found no surviving fixture workers or servers. The fixture now rejects an insufficient test deadline before starting processes, reserving its duration plus six minutes for recovery and cleanup. The CI workflow already uses `-timeout=18m`; the corrected local command uses the same timeout.

## Cancelable metadata handle caches

The journal stream/state and snapshot state/object caches previously held a mutex across network metadata lookups. A canceled follower could therefore wait behind the first request after its own context had expired, and a blocked stream/object lookup could hold up an unrelated state lookup. They now use a shared, context-aware handle cache per resource: one caller performs the lookup, other callers can cancel their waits independently, successful handles are cached and failed lookups remain retryable. No invocation data or journal entries are cached by this change.

A Tier 1 workload runs the production cache with two controlled waiters across all eight success/failure, waiter-identity and virtual cancellation/deadline combinations. It passed 100,000 seeds in 6.04 seconds, exact replay, cross-process identity and focused race/pinned checks; seed 42 is pinned. Six journal adapter cases cover each resource and independence of unrelated resources. Restoring the former production cache makes all six fail; the updated cache was restored afterward. Journal, simulator and worker suites passed (simulator 75.75 seconds), as did vet. Real three-node serial-response, manifest-response and snapshot purge/recovery contracts passed under the race detector in 20.70 seconds. A local race run of the earlier failing mixed seed 7 passed all 28 terminals and the history/integrity/queue gates, with terminal p99 17.96 seconds. This is a candidate contributor fix plus one local replay; it does not confirm the cause of the earlier 55.60-second CI miss or clear consecutive-seed validation.

## Sustained asymmetric worker reply isolation

`TestMixedMatrixWorkerReplyIsolationFortyFiveSeconds` adds a seventh sustained matrix selector (`isolation`). Three worker processes each use a distinct TCP proxy pinned to a different server and ignore discovered peers. The controller targets an active worker in seeded candidate order, holds server-to-worker replies for 45 seconds while requests continue upstream, then resumes replies. New proxy counters confirm held inbound bytes and increasing outbound bytes on the same active connection. A periodic worker PING marker and renewed inbound traffic confirm heal; an active isolation must report named fencing after the fault begins. Faults begin at +5 seconds and repeat every minute. The cluster keeps quorum, and workflow latency uses the raw enabling event.

The first 35-second workload race smoke passed one confirmed active fault, four fencing events, five batches, 140 terminal invocations and 1,541 journal entries. Aggregate terminal p99 was 2.84 seconds; all history/integrity/per-type latency and queue-drain gates passed. Its retained relay artifact showed one connection, client-to-server bytes increasing from 138,338 to 138,350 while 443 reply bytes were held, then restored inbound traffic and a successful worker PING after heal. The final helper/error-checking version also passed a race smoke in 66.92 seconds: one active fault, four fencing events, 140 terminals, 1,545 journal entries and aggregate terminal p99 3.01 seconds, with the same shared gates passed. This is shortened evidence; the ten-minute and consecutive-seed row remain open. A real three-node proxy contract verifies that the server receives an outbound request while its reply remains unavailable to the client, then receives exactly that held reply after heal. That contract and the existing serial/manifest network-response contracts passed under the race detector in 14.78 seconds; workflow YAML parsing and integration/testcluster vet passed.

Child dispatch/health-marker write failures now fail the helper, and the parent rejects retained child-test failure markers in addition to race-detector reports. A default temporary artifact prefix keeps that checking active when the caller omits an external artifact prefix. Cleanup resumes held replies before stopping workers and closing proxies.

## Bounded fault-selection metadata reads

Journal- and consumer-leader selection now retry named transient metadata replies up to three times with two-second requests and a cancelable 50-ms delay, within the existing twenty-second controller deadline. The seeded candidate order, actual kill requirement and recovery gates are unchanged. This addresses the earlier consumer seed 2 controller API 10008 failure; it does not address batch-result deadline failures. A controlled wire-response contract uses the real NATS SDK to decode API 10008, requires recovery after two transient responses, fails after three persistent responses and rejects missing-stream/unclassified API errors without retry. It passed under the race detector in 1.26 seconds. A shortened consumer seed 2 race run also passed all shared gates in 72.14 seconds; sustained consecutive-seed validation is still required.

The [full isolation run with server/relay capture at `37543b1`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36703375477) failed its first post-heal PING gate and retained all seven parent/server diagnostic files plus the affected worker stack. All three relays were waiting for input rather than blocked on their hold channels; the affected worker reader was waiting for input, while its metadata calls and PING awaited replies. The server snapshots contained no blocked mutex and no pending connection bytes. These are point-in-time observations, not a confirmed protocol cause or a green recovery cell. The retained connection counters and stacks support the next transport investigation without changing the gate.

The isolation fixture now captures a bounded connection transcript from before each worker connects: forwarded bytes in both directions, timestamps, connection IDs and relay endpoint addresses. The four-MiB budget per proxy includes record overhead; exhaustion stops capture and marks the transcript truncated. A truncated prefix cannot prove that a later reply was absent. On a controller failure these transcripts are retained beside the server/client/relay stacks. Workers advertise their process identity as the NATS connection name so `/connz` rows can be matched to relay upstream endpoints. The real asymmetric-response contract verifies request, reply and handshake capture, detached snapshot bytes, rejection of capture enabled after connecting, and continued forwarding with an exhausted capture budget. It passed under the race detector in 4.23 seconds; integration/testcluster vet passed. The capture-enabled shortened isolation race run passed all shared gates in 72.20 seconds. These additions gather protocol evidence; no production recovery fix or sustained CI pass is claimed.

## Complete isolation transcript and metadata-only contract

The [wire-capture isolation CI run at `adaacea`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36705145818) failed its first recovery gate. The affected proxy's transcript is untruncated and contains exactly one connection, matched by worker name and upstream endpoint to the server's connection record. Reassembling each direction and parsing NATS command lines with their declared payload lengths consumes the entire captured stream without a framing error: 67 forwarded client PINGs, 18 returned PONGs, 309,993 outbound bytes and 755,927 inbound bytes. At heal it forwards the buffered inbound prefix; no further inbound bytes appear during the ten-second recovery window, while fresh metadata requests continue upstream. The healthy proxies' transcripts are truncated and cannot support an equivalent completeness claim. This establishes unanswered protocol probes, but not why the server's reported outbound payload count exceeds the relay's actual forwarded bytes. Failure capture now also records loopback TCP queue/state data with bounded `ss -tinp`, because application pending-byte counters exclude the kernel send buffer.

`TestMetadataRecoveryAfterAsymmetricReplyHold` is a new opt-in three-process transport contract: 64 concurrent production-SDK `WF_RUN` metadata readers and the same periodic PING probe use one pinned proxy, hold replies for 45 seconds, then require a new PING and fresh metadata response within ten seconds. It removes workflow execution, leases, journal append decisions and dispatch while retaining the broker/SDK/relay boundaries. A local run passed in 51.93 seconds: 45.001-second hold, 21.46-ms recovery, 128 successful lookups and 448 expected timeout failures during the cut. This is a transport slice, not a sustained matrix row or explanation of the CI failure. The manual `metadata-isolation-contract` workflow retains the same wire/server/relay/socket diagnostics if the contract fails. Integration/testcluster vet and workflow YAML parsing passed.


## Pause selection race and isolation TCP queue evidence

The [twenty-seed pause run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36697735693) passed 19/20 seeds. Seed 7's fifth target recorded `released` at 09:57:50.383372579, before SIGSTOP at 09:57:50.383401874, but its separately updated active marker still reported one lease. There was no live execution to fence after resume. Pause selection now reads completed dispatch records after confirmed stop and checks retained KV ownership without modifying or renewing the lease. An idle stopped candidate is resumed and selection continues within the original five-second selection allowance. The 45-second hold and explicit fencing requirement remain. A regression covers the completed release with a stale active marker, ignores an incomplete final record, and rejects malformed completed records; its race run passed. A seed 7 race smoke passed in 70.66 seconds with one confirmed active pause, 196 terminals, 2,166 journal entries, aggregate terminal p99 5.03 seconds, and all shared gates. Integration vet and diff checks passed. This shortened run is excluded from ten-minute release evidence; fresh sustained validation remains required.

The [socket-enabled isolation run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36707159613) again failed the post-heal PING gate. The affected transcript maps proxy upstream `127.0.0.1:49032` to server `127.0.0.1:38599`. At failure the server socket has Send-Q 736,105 bytes, `notsent:734761`, retransmission backoff 7, and RTO 26,880 ms. Both relay sockets and the worker socket have empty receive/send queues. This locates outstanding bytes in the server's kernel TCP queue rather than its application pending-byte counter, and supports testing a reply-hold relay that continues draining upstream into a bounded buffer. It does not establish a NATS runtime bug or a completed fix.

The lost artifacts cannot supply socket evidence for this particular contract run. A fresh contract run is required.


## Bounded upstream-draining reply isolation

The [artifact-corrected metadata contract at `cb14933`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36708503003) reproduced the PING failure and retained its diagnostics. The matched server socket had Send-Q 694,523 bytes, `notsent:689399`, backoff 7 and RTO 25,984 ms while the relay upstream socket had empty queues. This independently reproduces the kernel-queue/backoff observation without workflow execution. The previous relay stopped reading upstream while holding one chunk, which introduced TCP backpressure into a test intended to hold application replies.

The reply-hold relay now continuously drains upstream into an ordered per-connection queue with an eight-MiB budget, including record overhead. It releases replies in order after heal; the reader and writer are independent. Overflow closes the connection and increments a sticky counter. Both sustained isolation and the metadata contract reject any overflow rather than counting reconnect as successful isolation recovery. Relay stats expose current and peak buffered payload bytes. Wire transcripts still record only bytes actually forwarded.

Race contracts verify a two-MiB reply drained during the hold while requests continue upstream, no held reply reaches the client, exact byte order after release, a repeated hold on the same connection, EOF-tail delivery, explicit overflow, and prompt close with queued replies. They passed in 1.13 seconds. The real asymmetric NATS contract and partition/reconnect contract passed under the race detector in 4.56 and 5.08 seconds; vet and diff checks passed. The metadata-only race contract passed in 53.83 seconds: 45.001-second hold, 22.30-ms recovery, 656,083-byte peak buffer and zero overflows. These are fixture and transport proofs; fresh CI metadata and sustained mixed isolation validation remain required. The ten-second PING, fencing, raw workflow latency and queue-drain gates are unchanged.

This 35-second workload is excluded from ten-minute evidence. ## Completed-cohort checkpoints while sustained workloads continue

The matrix generator previously waited for each whole-retained-state checkpoint before starting another batch. During a long checkpoint this deliberately left all workers idle while the pause controller still required an active target. Checkpoints now capture the `WF_INV` high-water mark after every tenth completed batch and queue that completed cohort to one independent reader. The generator immediately continues its same seeded mixed batches. Every queued checkpoint must finish before final validation; checkpoint failures cancel the workload and remain visible. The final quiescent audit still checks the entire retained state and exact totals.

`integrity.CheckThroughInvocationSequence` reads retained invocation records through the captured sequence, then checks those invocations' current journal and snapshot records and terminal KV values. Later invocations are outside that cohort. Cohort members must be quiescent and must not be purged or reused during the audit. The global checker remains required to detect journals outside the captured cohort and to establish final integrity. A real three-node race contract checks exclusion of later work, preservation of global orphan detection, and detection of corruption written to an older journal after the cutoff; it passed in 4.40 seconds. The integrity race suite, vet and diff checks passed.

## Reusable resolved promises with bounded result storage

`AwaitPromise` now consumes a child outcome signal once per replay and resolves subsequent awaits from that same outcome. Each returned result is detached, so caller mutation cannot change later awaits. Child failure and malformed-outcome errors remain reproducible. An object-store read failure leaves the consumed outcome available for another resolution attempt rather than waiting for a nonexistent second child signal. Cached resolved payloads are limited to sixteen MiB per context; results beyond that budget are reread and hash-verified. The outcome's existing signal payload remains the source for uncached resolution. Every replay reconstructs its own promise state; no cross-invocation cache is introduced.

SDK race contracts cover repeated success and replay, caller mutation, retry after an object-read failure, repeated child failure/corrupt outcome, and three six-MiB results exceeding the cache budget. The focused race checks passed in 1.16 seconds. Restoring the former production SDK makes the repeated-await regression suspend waiting for another signal. The production-worker child simulation now repeats the resolved await after mutating the first returned slice, across its existing child-start, journal, result, notification and consumer fault choices. It passed 100,000 seeds in 54.50 seconds, exact replay and cross-process identity; the pinned transport transcript remains unchanged because reuse adds no durable operation. The full simulator suite passed in 60.08 seconds. Final SDK/worker suites passed in 1.06/13.09 seconds; vet and diff checks passed.

The real three-node five-child fan-out now also awaits each promise again after mutating its first returned result. It passed under the race detector in 5.57 seconds with correct parent result and retained integrity. This proves reusable outcomes for that contract; general durable select and the other promise API refinements remain open.


## General durable select across SDK awaitables

`wf.Select` accepts any combination of SDK timer handles, named signal
awaitables and child promises. The first ready argument wins; request identity,
argument order and the selected case/sequence are durable and checked on replay.
A replay uses its recorded completion rather than reevaluating readiness.
Losers remain usable, and callers explicitly cancel unwanted timers. Repeated
resolution of a selected promise uses the same durable child outcome. Empty,
nil, invalid, canceled and already-fired cases fail before journaling.
The suspended-state scanner reads the complete pending case list and repairs
when any timer, signal or promise is ready; an unavailable signal read does not
suppress an independently ready case. Existing timer/signal select journals
retain their original protocol.

SDK race contracts cover suspension, replay, loser reuse, changed ordering,
invalid cases, corrupt completions and a committed selection with a lost
acknowledgment. Real three-node race contracts exercise signal and timer winners
across worker restart, and an actual child-promise winner after the parent run
wakeup is deleted and repaired by the suspended scanner. The seeded SDK/journal
slice passed 100,000 schedules in 11.37 seconds, exact and cross-process replay,
and focused race/pinned checks. Buffered events are model fixture inputs;
full worker/scanner/child-notifier simulation for general select remains open.
Materialized state checkpoints and broader fault/release gates remain open.

## Deterministic balanced assignment policy

`assignment.Plan` now balances all 64 partitions over a supplied live worker
snapshot. Members are sorted, quotas differ by at most one, and existing owners
retain their lowest numbered partitions up to their quota. Only dead/unlisted
owners and excess partitions move. The plan minimizes moves for those fixed
quotas and is independent of membership input order. Inputs are not mutated.
`assignment.Rebalance` reads every retained owner/revision, supports dry run,
and applies the plan with revision CAS. A concurrent move is not overwritten;
conflicts are deferred to the next pass. Unknown acknowledgments remain errors
and a later pass discovers any committed change without blindly repeating it.

Property contracts cover membership sizes 1–64, deterministic ordering, exact
quotas, minimum move counts, invalid inputs and a stable converged pass. A real
three-node race contract covers unchanged dry-run state, a competing CAS move,
a committed move with a hidden acknowledgment, recovery without another write
to that partition, and a deleted assignment key. The complete assignment race
suite passed in 3.74 seconds; vet and diff checks passed.

Initial attempts timed out during eager cluster metadata/bucket provisioning,
before assignment operations. The fixture now waits through bounded
AccountInfo and assignment-bucket readiness calls, matching existing integration
fixture startup behavior. This does not establish a NATS defect.

The API currently requires an authoritative membership snapshot from its caller.
Worker heartbeat registration, expiry-based membership, coordinator ownership,
and automatic runner integration remain to be implemented; this policy is the
assignment step for that controller, not a completed automatic rebalance claim.


## Expiring membership and automatic worker assignment

`assignment.EnsureMembership` creates and verifies the optional `WF_MEMBERS`
bucket with the production twelve-second TTL, three-second renewal cadence,
file storage and configured replication. It reuses the production lease
registration, epoch and revision-fencing code. Worker IDs are hashed into keys;
retained values preserve the original ID. Live membership uses server expiry
rather than comparing worker wall clocks, excludes uninitialized registrations,
and rejects malformed retained entries. Duplicate live IDs cannot register.
An expired process cannot renew or delete a reused ID's successor epoch.

A membership controller holds a separate coordinator lease in that bucket,
reads live registrations, and applies the balanced revision-CAS plan. It renews
coordinator ownership before each move. Passes have an eight-second bound;
registration or transport errors return to the runner, which cancels and joins
its worker and repair loops. Cleanup uses retained revisions, with expiry as
its crash backstop. `wf-worker -mode auto` registers before starting consumers,
follows `WF_ASSIGN`, and joins its controller before releasing registration.
Every member must supply the same workflow handler set. This optional bucket
is created only by automatic deployments; the default static mode is preserved.

Focused contracts exercise actual server expiry, duplicate ID rejection,
successor epoch fencing, configuration mismatch rejection, balanced joins and
graceful leaves, and retained coordinator/membership expiry before takeover.
The runner smoke covers automatic assignment, workflow completion, metrics and
shutdown. Full process-kill/partition/clock-skew matrix coverage of automatic
membership and a seeded membership snapshot/controller transport remain open.
The existing rebalance fault matrix still exercises explicit assignment moves.

The complete assignment race suite passed in 40.32 seconds; the final focused
join/leave/retained-expiry takeover race passed in 25.26 seconds. The runner's
static, KV and automatic workflow/metrics smoke passed under the race detector
in 5.67 seconds. Assignment/runner package suites and vet/diff checks passed.
These are focused membership/controller and one-node runner contracts, not a
sustained automatic-membership chaos or full-matrix release proof.

## Thirty-day native timer firing after full restarts and clock advance

The five-container fixture now supports a separately compiled advanced-clock
server, initially unused. Its Go `time.Now` wall component advances by a bounded
1–31-day offset while preserving the monotonic component. The existing ±60-second
skew injector keeps its original validation. Switching all peers to the future
clock requires every container to be stopped and removed; an attempted live
switch is rejected before changing the fixture state.

`TestFiveContainerThirtyDayTimerFiresAfterTwoRestarts` journals a real native
thirty-day sleep, retains its schedule, and stops its worker. After the first
full SIGKILL/restart, all five server clocks remain unshifted, the exact journal
prefix and deadline survive, and no target wakeup exists. After the second full
SIGKILL, all peers restart on the same file stores with their Go clocks advanced
by 31 days. The fixture verifies each actual process clock through `/varz`, checks
the unchanged journal, requires a generated wakeup with a timestamp after the
recorded deadline, and runs a replacement worker. It checks the five-entry
terminal journal, Start/Await histories and retained-state integrity. The final
contract also reads the same result through every restarted node.

The first normal run passed in 49.78 seconds with 57.4 ms post-readiness
completion; the first race run passed in 36.77 seconds with 90.3 ms completion.
The deliberate clock jump places the deadline about one virtual day in the past;
these recovery times measure readiness-to-completion, not raw deadline lateness
or an ordinary fault-matrix latency cell. This supplies the advanced-clock
thirty-day firing proof. Sustained timer faults, the full skew matrix, native
schedule volume and the complete Tier 3 soak remain independent gates.

The nightly/manual `tier3-container-smoke` workflow now has a dedicated
`long-timer-clock` race job and a client-history artifact for this proof.

Final combined race controls passed in 131.70 seconds: the original 16-timer
restart proof retained all 80 entries with 261 ms recovery, and the advanced
thirty-day test passed in 41.22 seconds with 195 ms recovery. Its exported
history contains one Start and six terminal reads, including all five nodes.
The complete testcluster package passed in 23.97 seconds; vet and diff checks
passed. These are local proofs; the dedicated new CI job still needs validation.

## Real five-second block-device stalls

`testcluster.BlockDisk` creates a private 512 MiB sparse image, loop device,
device-mapper linear target and ext4 mount. It never maps a host data device.
The sustained `blockdisk` row places node 2's entire JetStream store on this
filesystem, moves the six relevant workflow stream leaders there before each
thirty-second fault, suspends all mapped-device I/O for five seconds, and
requires full replica catch-up after resume. Each fault captures device state,
suspend/resume times and a dirty-file sync that remained blocked for the full
interval. This covers newly created files as well as existing files, unlike
the path-filtered strace injector. The shared histories, raw-state audits,
raw enabling-event p99 and queue-drain gates remain required.

The privileged fixture race test passed in 6.56 seconds, including a five-second
blocked-sync proof, cancellation recovery, and removal of the mount, mapping,
loop device and image. The first attempt found that this VM does not populate
`/dev/mapper` automatically after target creation; the fixture now uses the
explicit documented `dmsetup mknodes` operation. A seed 42 matrix race smoke
passed in 68.42 seconds: eight batches, 224 terminals, all shared gates and
aggregate terminal p99 4.999 seconds. The device remained suspended for 5.014
seconds, and the dirty sync returned 5.043 seconds after suspension. No test
mappings or loop devices remained after cleanup. Vet and diff checks passed.
This is 35-second smoke evidence, not sustained or consecutive-seed validation.

CI exposes `blockdisk` with 1/20/200 seeds and first runs the privileged fixture
race test. Passwordless sudo, loop devices, device mapper and ext4 tools are
required. This VM's kernel has no `dm-delay` target or loadable module; the
[distinct per-request delay injection](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/device-mapper/delay.html)
required by Tier 3 remains open, as does the five-node full-matrix soak.

sixteen, including snapshot reconstruction and terminal KV agreement. Previously
this phase ran serially after the concurrent raw scan, so a stalled KV leader
could consume a checkpoint allowance while checking thousands of terminal
values. Results are reduced in sorted subject order; a faster later request
cannot hide an earlier invariant error or change the reported failing subject.
Every invocation/journal/snapshot/terminal check remains required. The per-read
two-second attempts, named transient retry policy, twenty-second matrix audit
attempts and overall matrix latency/completion gates are unchanged.

and missing terminal values in a later window, structural corruption in the

returns sooner. The complete integrity package passed under the race detector

contracts passed in a 12.79-second integration run. The explicitly enabled
33,600-entry/800-terminal scale proof passed under its twenty-second audit
deadline in 13.58 seconds (24.35 seconds total Go test time). A new scale shape
matching larger terminal cohorts passed 3,200 invocations, 3,200 terminal values
and 32,000 entries under the same deadline in 12.93 seconds (25.03 seconds total).
Both scale shapes are now included in the per-push audit job. Vet and diff
checks passed. These no-fault proofs do not explain or clear the earlier

## Isolation target selection race in the 200-seed campaign

The [200-seed isolation campaign](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36718010557)
failed seeds 21, 29 and 37 with `isolated active worker reported no fencing`.
Downloaded fault/dispatch artifacts show releases at the selection boundary:
seed 21's short deliveries released 77–79 ms before the cut; seed 29's selected
signal released 83 microseconds before it; seed 37's last signal release event
was timestamped 14 microseconds afterward. The active marker and actual release
can cross because the observer persists its marker after the release operation.
These runs do not provide active-execution fencing proof or a clean release gate.

Isolation selection now arms the subprocesses and waits at a newly acquired
delivery boundary. The selected delivery cannot execute or release its lease
until the parent installs its reply hold. All acquisition barriers are then
released immediately; the chosen proxy alone holds replies for 45 seconds.
The fault artifact records a fresh token, invocation, run sequence and delivery
number. The fencing reader requires a post-cut lost-lease/stale-journal error
from that exact delivery, excluding unrelated invocations and earlier delivery
attempts. The acquisition barrier is bounded and selection failure disarms it.
The production worker implementation is unchanged.

Race tests reject stale readiness markers, premature handoff, canceled selection
and unrelated fencing evidence. A seed-21 real race smoke passed in 74.82 seconds;
a seed-29 race smoke with the delivery-specific fencing gate passed in 69.71
seconds. Both retain the existing histories, integrity, latency and queue-drain
gates. A ten-minute seed-21 race replay is in progress; shortened proofs do not
clear sustained or consecutive-seed release requirements.

The [new full Tier 1 CI run](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36741786098)
at `493c6a7` is live with 100,000 seeds per workload, including the WorkQueue
retention extension. It remains separate from the completed expanded run above.


## Mixed-version retention after a stream-leader move

The new `mixed-move-after-ack` opt-in control reproduces the 33-record retained
state with the runtime's inherited consumer replicas. It waits the unchanged
thirty-second drain allowance, requires ack floor 33 and no consumer pending
work, and saves a complete raw sequence scan containing every record. Only then
does it move the stream leader onto the upgraded consumer leader's node.
Without republishing or issuing new acknowledgments, the retained stream drains
and consumer progress remains complete. The initial local race test passed in 43.70
seconds. The final test additionally verifies the expected leader placement
before and after the move and reads each original sequence afterward; all 33
must return message-not-found. That final race test passed in 40.57 seconds.
One intervening attempt failed before ack at preferred consumer-leader placement.
The helper now waits for all peers to be current and retries the documented
preferred stepdown request within its existing ten-second bound; the unchanged
thirty-second retention requirement remains strict. This proves that recovery action in the fixture, not that arbitrary
leader changes repair all mixed-version queues or that release gates are green.

A likely compatibility mechanism is now visible in pinned upstream source:
[2.11.17 `stream.ackMsg`](https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/blob/v2.11.17/server/stream.go)
allows a consumer leader to propose retention removal; [2.15.0](https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/blob/v2.15.0/server/stream.go)
assigns that responsibility to the stream leader. In the failing placement, the
upgraded consumer leader is a stream follower and the old stream leader is a
consumer follower, leaving neither eligible under its own rule. This is an
inference from the real placement controls and source, not yet branch-level
instrumentation or an upstream compatibility patch. The ordinary split-version
contracts still fail strictly, and the full upgrade matrix keeps seeded node
order. No automatic production repair or queue purge has been added.

## Two-consumer mixed-version retention and CI controls

The new `TestMixedVersionMultipleConsumerRetentionRecovery` uses two independent
R3 consumer groups with inherited replicas on one WorkQueue stream. Each fetches
33 records before one consumer leader upgrades. Both groups acknowledge out of
order using confirmed DoubleAck. After thirty seconds, both consumers have zero
pending work and completed ack floors, but only the upgraded leader's 33 records
remain stored under the old stream leader. The old consumer leader's records
are absent. Individual raw reads and a complete saved stream scan verify this
per-group distinction; it is not a counter-only comparison.

Moving the stream leader onto the upgraded node removes the retained group.
The other consumer leader then upgrades and receives a second 33-record cohort
alongside the first group. Both cohorts drain with separate upgraded consumer
leaders, one remote from the upgraded stream leader. Every one of the 132
original stream sequences must return message-not-found, consumer ack floors
must match all deliveries, and the expected final leaders and versions must be
confirmed. The initial local race proof passed in 44.99 seconds. This strengthens
the placement/ownership hypothesis and recovery controls without claiming a
production repair protocol or closing split-version conformance.

raw state on successful runs and server logs on failures. It has a manual
trigger and runs on changes to these contracts, the process fixture or module

## Lease serialization deadlines and seeded cancellation reproduction

A later [mixed-fault CI campaign](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36744596798)
at `ba5c625` passed seed 1 and failed seed 2 with terminal p99 63.13 seconds.
Its signals and timers made journal progress interspersed with failed renewal,
lease-loss and retry events while the syscall disk delay remained active.
The route recovery timestamp already applies the user's later-of-enable/heal
rule; the disk fault intentionally continues through completion. This remains
a failed latency gate, not a route-timestamp definition fix.

Inspection found a separate local deadline defect: Renew, Release and Cleanup
held one mutex across their network calls, so a waiting operation could exceed
its own context deadline while another operation held the mutex. Lease revision
decisions now use a cancellable gate. Cancellation before gate acquisition
makes no KV request and leaves ownership unchanged; an uncertain renewal that
actually attempted its update still marks the owner lost. Serialization and
revision CAS remain required.

The new Tier 1 workload holds a production renewal, starts one of the three
contending operations, delivers virtual cancellation/deadline and verifies
prompt independent return, no transport access, and unchanged ownership from
the canceled wait. A failed held renewal must remain fenced; a successful one
must permit a later renewal. All twelve combinations are seeded. The old-mutex
build overlay fails seed 1, exact replay and cross-process identity pass, and
seed 42 is pinned. The final 100,000-seed run passed in 4.08 seconds; the full
simulator suite passed in 49.97 seconds, lease tests in 1.16 seconds, and final
pinned race corpus in 1.96 seconds. Vet and diff checks passed.

The local seed-2 four-fault race replay passed in 62.91 seconds with terminal
p99 23.419 seconds across 28 invocations. This is a fresh local passing result,
not controlled attribution of the old CI miss or a replacement consecutive
seed gate. Materialized SDK state checkpoints remain open; this investigation
took priority when the new CI failure appeared.

The [standard test run at `ba5c625`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36744596826)
failed its 10,000-round CAS proof after the independent retained audit had read

available for request`. This is incomplete audit evidence, not a demonstrated
second CAS winner or missing record. The production long-journal reader already
has separate modeled no-responder/partial-delivery recovery.

The independent raw CAS audit now preserves its verified count, stream sequence
and epoch across a named transient consumer failure. A replacement ordered
consumer starts at the last verified sequence plus one; partial-batch entries
are checked before its error is handled. At most three consecutive recovery
attempts without progress are allowed, inside the unchanged three-minute audit
context. No responders, consumer-deleted, request timeout, no-stream-response
and API 10008 are named transport cases. Semantic errors fail directly,
including semantic errors wrapped or joined with a transport error. Creation
attempts still rotate through pinned nodes within their original bounds, and
semantic creation failures are not retried.

Controlled transport tests prove continuation after partial delivery, correct
restart position, bounded persistent failure and rejection of missing,
duplicate, corrupt and unexpected-writer entries. A wrapped semantic error
after delivery of every expected entry must still fail. The final focused race
checks passed in 1.27 seconds; integration vet and diff checks passed.

The full local 10,000-round proof passed in 66.79 seconds with twenty leader
kills, no unknown winner rounds or pre-publication retries, and all 10,001
retained entries audited. The separate production read returned the same full
journal and tail in 313 ms. The final tail/count, retained stream counts,
entry index/kind/worker, sequence and epoch assertions remain strict. This
repairs the audit's handling of a transient response; it does not identify
why the server/client consumer returned no responders in the old CI run or
replace fresh clean-runner validation.


## Shared retained-journal checker negative controls

The invariant review found five mutations that survived `CheckSnapshot`:
zero, duplicate and descending stream sequences, an unknown entry kind, and a
successful terminal after an unresolved step request. The real checker already
checked sequences separately; sequence validation now lives in the shared
journal checker so real and simulated retained state enforce the same rule.
Global stream-sequence holes remain valid. Unknown kinds and successful
completion with a pending request now fail directly. Failed terminals may
retain a pending request, as cancellation and journal-limit failure require;
nonterminal pending and suspended histories remain valid intermediate cuts.

The new controls failed against the previous checker before the fix. Real
three-node race controls also reject an unknown kind and unresolved successful
terminal, while accepting a failed pending step; the focused integrity/cohort
integration run passed in 17.14 seconds. The complete integrity race suite
passed in 1.88 seconds; vet and diff checks passed. The complete simulator race
run is still active, with its result pending. These are added checker controls, not
completion of the release's six production mutation campaign requirements.

The [standard CI run at `af26451`](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36747611863)
and its [20-seed mixed campaign](https://github.com/AntPAllen/js-wf/actions/runs/36747612041)
